articles.title: Christa Pike is ‘up and walking’ for first time after failed execution, lawyer says
articles.summary:
Recovery marks a dramatic turnaround for Pike, who remains in hospital after a botched execution in Tennessee

Christa Pike is “up and walking” in hospital, her lawyer said, just more than a…

blocks.text: Christa Pike is “up and walking” in hospital, her lawyer said, just more than a week after she survived two lethal injections during a botched execution in Tennessee.

The recovery marks a dramatic turnaround after Pike was declared brain dead on Monday, before waking up and beginning to speak on Tuesday. Her ordeal has shocked many in the US and overseas and galvanized critics of the death penalty.

Stephen Ferrell, a lawyer on Pike’s legal team, told the BBC that she was able to walk, but remained mentally foggy. “What’s been described to me is that physically there’s quite a bit going on, that her arms are very injured and she’s not able to use them very much,” Ferrell said.
“She is up and walking for the first time today, but just around the room, not very far,” he added.
Pike, 50, was taken to hospital unconscious but alive from Tennessee’s execution chamber on 30 September, after receiving two doses of the barbiturate pentobarbital.

After the botched execution attempt, one of her lawyers called the process “cruel and torturous”, adding that he had counted seven needles in Pike’s left arm, “one of which appeared to be bent when it was pulled from her”. Pike had lifted her head from the execution gurney to say her arms were burning as the drug was administered.
Pike’s team is seeking psychological support for her, given that “clearly is necessary now”, Ferrell said. On Wednesday, Pike was described as “angry and confused” after regaining consciousness.

Ferrell said of Pike’s mental state: “I think it’s kind of good and bad. Good that she is fairly with it, but she’s also somewhat foggy. She can lose her train of thought really easily and forgets where she’s going.”
He said it remains to be seen whether Pike makes a full recovery.
“I assume [Pike’s condition] will keep improving, but there could be some permanent damage. We don’t know that yet.”

On Wednesday Randy Spivey, another attorney for Pike, said she was unable to move her arms and has pneumonia and a blood clot. Despite her condition, Pike was still being restrained, her team said, shackled to her hospital bed by her feet and right arm.

Pike’s lawyers had warned before the execution that officials might struggle to locate veins and cause her suffering in the process, but the state had pushed to proceed and the US supreme court allowed the prison to move forward.

There is speculation from medical experts that perhaps some or a lot of the drug missed her vein and went into tissue, that one of her veins, which were problematic and this fact flagged by her lawyers months earlier – blew, or that the drug was faulty, or a combination.
Pike was 18 and her then boyfriend 17 at the time when they killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, one of their classmates at Knoxville Job Corps, in Tennessee in 1995.
According to prosecutors, Pike was worried Slemmer was trying to take the boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, away from her. Together, they lured Slemmer into a wooded area, tortured and killed her.

Shipp was convicted of first-degree murder in 1997 and was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole. Pike has never denied her involvement in Slemmer’s killing. She was later diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder but, because she was 18, she was sentenced to death and has been on death row, isolated, for 30 years.

Pike’s attorneys have argued that her original legal team failed to present evidence about the sexual and physical abuse she suffered during childhood. Tennessee’s governor, Bill Lee, blocked Pike’s request for clemency. He has since halted the state’s remaining executions for the rest of the year and has ordered a “comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred”.

articles.title: First Thing: Trump endures protests in Texas as DNC sues over adverts
articles.summary:
The president was repeatedly interrupted at a rally and faces a legal challenge over taxpayer-funded adverts. Plus Jonathan, the giant tortoise who may have the secret to longevity

Good…

blocks.text: Good morning. Donald Trump suffered a torrid night at a rally in Texas that was rocked by repeated protests. The US president briefly stepped away from the microphone after one protester appeared to approach the stage. At least half a dozen demonstrators interrupted Trump during his remarks in San Antonio, with some led away by police. One was physically assaulted by an older Trump supporter as he tried to leave the arena.

items: What is the latest development in the saga over taxpayer-funded pro-Trump ads? The Democratic National Committee has sued the Trump administration in federal court, asking a judge in Washington to stop the president from using taxpayer funds to air a series of ads promoting himself. The ads have cost taxpayers more than $12m so far, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact.

Why has Trump been forced to distance himself from two top aides? Trump claimed he did not have “any idea who else they work for” after it was reported that Chris LaCivita, the co-manager of his 2024 presidential campaign, and James Blair, a campaign adviser and White House deputy chief of staff on leave of absence, spent the weekend assisting the pro-Russia government in Republika Srpska in the Balkans. Trump said: “I will terminate them, immediately” if he determined there was a conflict of interest.

blocks.text: Tanker attacked off Qatar as Ken Paxton admits Iran war and gas prices are plaguing Republicans

blocks.caption: Vessels in the strait of Hormuz. Photograph: Amirhosein Khorgooi/Isna/Wana//Reuters

blocks.text: A tanker sailing off the north coast of Qatar has been attacked, causing an unknown number of casualties. It came as Iran declared it would close a route in the strait of Hormuz being used to circumvent Tehran’s blockade of traffic.

Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general running as the Republican candidate in a competitive Senate race, admitted in a leaked audio recording that rising fuel prices as a result of Trump’s Iran war were hurting his party before the midterms. The Guardian has asked Paxton’s campaign for comment.

items: What is the latest in the diplomatic dispute between the UK and Israel? Britain is rebranding its East Jerusalem consulate as a UK mission. The move was forced by the Israeli government as punishment for Britain’s decision to ban trade with illegal settlements. There has been some dispute within the UK government over whether taking tough measures at this time against Israel could help Benjamin Netanyahu’s re-election prospects this month.

blocks.text: WHO says it does not have ‘full picture’ from Russia after suspected plague death

blocks.caption: Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the World Health Organization’s director general.  Photograph: Fabrice Coffrini/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The World Health Organization has said it does not have the “full picture” from Russia after the suspected death from plague last week of a 28-year-old laboratory worker in Siberia. Russian authorities have denied a connection with the anti-plague research institute and say Darya Shipilova died from “pneumonia of an unknown aetiology”. They insist there is no danger of a plague outbreak and have described the “sanitary and epidemiological” situation in the region as stable.

items: What did the WHO director general say? At a press conference, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said: “We don’t yet have the full picture of this event. Timely, complete and transparent information-sharing is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public risks.”

What action has Russia appeared to have taken? Officials have imposed sweeping quarantine restrictions at the lab where Shipilova worked and in nearby hospitals. Staff were locked down inside the institute for three days, sleeping on the floors and on chairs, while tests were conducted.

blocks.text: Christa Pike ‘angry, confused’ and unable to move arms after failed execution, lawyers say

blocks.caption: Randy Spivey, an attorney for Christa Pike. Photograph: George Walker IV/AP

blocks.text: Christa Pike had woken up “angry and confused” after surviving two lethal injections, her attorneys said. Pike remains hospitalized and shackled to her bed. She has pneumonia and a blood clot, and is unable to move either of her badly injured arms. Randy Spivey, one of her lawyers, said her first words were: “Where am I?”, adding: “I think she is angry and confused about everything right now.” A judge has ordered Tennessee state officials to preserve all evidence related to the failed execution. Pike was convicted for her part in the 1995 brutal murder of Colleen Slemmer.

articles.title: Three sisters who drowned in Brighton took their own lives, inquest finds
articles.summary:
Jane Adetoro, Christina Walters and Rebecca Walters from London visited late mother’s former home shortly before their deaths in May

Three sisters who drowned in the sea in Brighton…

blocks.text: Three sisters who drowned in the sea in Brighton collectively decided to end their own lives, a coroner has ruled.
The bodies of Jane Adetoro, 36, Christina Walters, 32, and Rebecca Walters, 31, all from London, were recovered from the sea off Brighton in the early hours of 13 May.

An inquest into their deaths heard on Thursday that in the days before they died, the three women made a trip together to Birmingham to visit the former home of their mother, who died by drowning in 2010.

The inquest at Woodvale coroner’s court in Brighton heard that the sisters travelled by taxi to Birmingham on 11 May and were dropped off at 11.36pm at Linton Walk. The address is close to Brookvale Park Lake, where their mother, Janice Adetoro, died. They were picked up to return to the flat they lived in together in Greenford, west London, at 1.28am on 12 May.
DCI Mark Cullimore, of Sussex police, told the hearing there was no CCTV to show what the women did in the time they were in Birmingham.
On the evening of 12 May, they took a pre-booked taxi to Brighton and arrived near the seafront at 10.21pm. They are thought to have last been seen alive on CCTV from the beach at 2.42am on 13 May.
The bodies of Jane Adetoro and Christina Walters were located by a RNLI lifeboat crew; Rebecca Walters’ body was recovered from the shoreline on Brighton beach.
The senior coroner Penelope Schofield told the court on Thursday: “In hours of darkness, they entered the sea at Brighton, they could not swim and sea conditions were adverse.”
A postmortem found all three women had drowned. There was no evidence of any drugs or alcohol in their bodies and no evidence to suggest they had been subjected to violence.
The coroner concluded that the medical cause of death for all three women was drowning and that they had died by suicide.

Schofield told the court: “These three sisters lived very secluded lives, they were incredibly private. We don’t know why they took this course of action or indeed why they chose to do it in Brighton. It is not for the court to speculate and sadly these reasons may never be known.”

The inquest heard that Christina Walters had suffered from anxiety and depression since her mother’s death, but no such issues were recorded for her sister Rebecca. Adetoro was not registered with a doctor.

The women’s father, Joseph Jacobson, who attended the hearing by video link, said in a written statement: “There are no words that can adequately express the pain of losing a child. To lose all three of my precious daughters, Jane, Christina and Rebecca, is a heartbreak beyond anything I could ever have imagined.”

He said he could not understand why their lives had ended so suddenly, adding: “You were my daughters, you will always be my daughters and I will love you for the rest of my life. May your beautiful souls rest in perfect peace.”

items: In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org

articles.title: S. Korea warns of AI-aided hacking after bank data breaches
articles.summary: Seoul is alarmed after a recent breach of South Korean banks' cyber defenses that reportedly involved AI-assisted hacking. Officials warn such methods could be used to also target other sectors and…

image.caption: Image: Loïc Déquier/PHOTOPQR/SUD OUEST/picture alliance

blocks.text: The South Korean government has demanded a comprehensive overhaul of safeguards against hackers after seven of the nation's major financial institutions' cyber defenses were breached last week and the private data of thousands of customers was leaked.

The data breaches go beyond the financial sector, with two of the largest churches in the country and Korea Electric Power Corp. on Wednesday confirming that their online systems had been illegally accessed, although it is not clear whether the same perpetrator was responsible for all the attacks.
On Tuesday, Prime Minister Han Seong-sook called for measures to be taken swiftly to halt any further leaks.

"This is a serious situation because this incident is believed to have taken advantage of artificial intelligence, and if AI is used in phishing attacks, it could lead to secondary damage," Yonhap News quoted Han as saying at a Cabinet meeting.
"It is also a serious situation in that similar hacking methods could spread beyond the financial sector to industries, as well as government and public sectors."
Cyberattacks: How secure are smart devices really?
Threats to other sectors
Han said government agencies, public institutions, the financial sector and private enterprises all need to "remain vigilant."

Early reports from the US-based cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike suggest that the attack may have originated in China, although South Korea's Financial Supervisory Service (FSS) said it had identified 28 internet protocol addresses in the United States, Japan, Germany and at least 10 other countries that were involved in the bank breaches.
"South Korea officials are being careful about how they are framing their findings," said Aditya Das, an analyst at cryptocurrency research firm Brave New Coin in Auckland, New Zealand.
In the bank logs, investigators found traces of a tool called ARTEX, an open-source "autonomous penetration-testing" agent built by a Chinese developer, he said.

"It is freely available on the internet and officials have said explicitly that a Chinese-built tool doesn't mean Chinese attackers," Das told DW, adding that the use of multiple IP addresses is likely to be "a ploy by the hackers to hide their tracks."
It appears that the hackers exploited weak authentication protocols in portals used by external loan recruiters, employees' mobile tools and sales-support systems.
How much are hackers making?
Data on thousands of customers lost

According to South Korean media reports, data belonging to as many as 68,000 customers was taken, with Shinhan Bank, KB Kookmin Bank and Hana Bank among the worst affected. Names, phone numbers, annual income figures, loan limits and their loan products were accessed, along with a small number of national identification numbers.

Das pointed out that if a scammer has a person's name, phone number, income figure and is aware that the individual has recently applied for a loan, a fake "bank security" call can be very convincing to the unwary. Once a victim has transferred funds to an account specified by the scammer, it is very difficult to get it back.
Hyobin Lee, a professor at Sogang University in Seoul, says the seriousness of the incident goes far beyond the simple exposure of personal information.
"If criminals obtain such information, they may be able to carry out sophisticated financial fraud, identity theft, or highly targeted phishing attacks," she said.

"Another concern is that stolen personal information can be reused or combined with other leaked databases, potentially creating security risks that persist long after the original attack," Lee underlined.
"More broadly, such incidents can undermine public confidence in financial institutions and raise concerns about the security of the financial system as a whole."

While major financial institutions have invested heavily in protecting their core systems, such as internet banking and mobile banking platforms, Lee said they have overlooked other elements of their networks.

"Some auxiliary systems, such as loan agent information portals and internal mobile applications used by employees, appear to have received less security attention," she said, adding that the application of AI by the hackers is another concerning element.
Is AI the new weapon of mass data theft?
AI makes hacking easier?

"In the past, identifying security vulnerabilities, developing malicious code and conducting attacks against financial institutions required substantial technical expertise and considerable time," Lee pointed out. "Today, generative AI tools can assist with writing computer code, analyzing software vulnerabilities, processing large amounts of information and automating certain stages of cyber operations."

AI is "lowering the technical barriers to cybercrime" and making it accessible to more bad actors. At the same time, the technology is ramping up the speed and scale of attacks to overwhelm cyber defenses.
Given those developments, Lee fears that AI-assisted cyberattacks are only going to become more frequent.

"And the risks will not be limited to financial institutions," she said. "Hospitals, government agencies, energy infrastructure, telecommunications networks and other organizations holding sensitive information may also become increasingly attractive targets."

articles.title: Can Sánchez convince Spanish voters he is their best hope for fairer housing?
articles.summary: Recent death of 87-year-old woman likely to focus attention on crisis in run-up to general election at end of November

blocks.text: Even before María del Carmen Abascal died on Wednesday night, a mere fortnight after her eviction from the Madrid flat where she had lived for most of her life, the frail 87-year-old woman had become the enduring face of Spain’s housing crisis.

Her plight – and the wider issue it embodied – had led to street demonstrations, the creation of a protest camp in the middle of the Spanish capital, and spurred the socialist-led government to propose emergency measures to facilitate and protect access to housing. When rightwing and far-right parties voted down those measures in congress last week, the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, responded by announcing a snap general election for the end of November.

blocks.caption: Flowers and candles are placed in memory of María del Carmen Abascal at a housing protest camp in Puerta del Sol, Madrid, on Thursday.  Photograph: Borja Sanchez-Trillo/EPA

blocks.text: Abascal’s death now looks set to focus even more attention on housing in the run-up to that election and, in particular, on what her lawyer has called “the shameful violence of these types of evictions and the evident impact and consequences they can have on people’s health”.

With more than 42% of Spaniards identifying access to housing as their main worry and with rents having risen by 80% over the past decade, the most pertinent question may be: why has it taken the eviction of an octogenarian and the accompanying protests to shake Spain’s political class into action? To which the answer could be that, despite years of protests against overtourism and gentrification, the tipping point had not been reached. Now, arguably, it has.

On Thursday, Spain’s state centre for sociological research published polling that showed that 76.3% of those surveyed were in favour of the state intervening in the market “as much as necessary to guarantee everyone’s access to housing”, while 79% believed housing should be prioritised as a constitutional right.

Sánchez’s socialist-led government is keen to persuade voters that it is the only political force that cares about rents and tenants’ rights – hence the emergency measures, which have been redrafted into two new decrees after their defeat in parliament last week. The 21 measures include facilitating renting or buying a new home; extending eviction protections for vulnerable residents; prohibiting speculative real estate purchases, and granting tax breaks to property owners and tenants who pay on time.

blocks.caption: Pedro Sánchez: ‘a matter of simple common sense; a matter of humanity’. Photograph: Burak Akbulut/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: “These are measures that, if I may say so, are a matter of simple common sense; a matter of humanity,” the prime minister said on Tuesday. “They unite small property owners and tenants while standing up to vulture funds, precisely because they target only those who view housing merely as a commodity for speculation.”

The measures come almost three years after the prime minister promised to build 184,000 affordable public rental homes. His government has also sought to address soaring housing prices by introducing a law allowing authorities to cap “disproportionate” rent prices in some areas.

Those who had voted down last week’s decrees, Sánchez said, had done so despite studies showing the measures enjoyed “cross-cutting support that transcends ideology”, adding that the public was in favour of regulating “a dysfunctional market”. He is now hoping that at least one of the decrees will be passed by congress’s permanent council, a special body that operates when parliament is not in session. Its approval could go some way to convincing voters that his administration is taking the housing issue seriously.

blocks.caption: The leader of Spain’s right-wing opposition People’s party, Alberto Núñez Feijóo (centre), has promised to address the crisis despite his party voting against the proposed measures last week. Photograph: Antonio Sempere/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Others disagree. Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party, which voted down the measures last week, has said it is a bit late for Sánchez, who has been prime minister since 2018, to suddenly appoint himself Spain’s housing champion.

“Housing has been the big failure of this government but will be the success story of the one that follows it,” he said on Monday. Feijóo, whose party is leading the polls, added: “When a prime minister has been in power for eight years, it’s hard to blame others for what he’s failed to do.” The PP has promised to address the crisis by building 200,000 homes a year, lowering taxes and cutting down on bureaucracy.
after newsletter promotion

However, the PP’s decision to side with the far-right Vox party and the rightwing Catalan pro-independence Junts party to fell the measures has left it looking less than committed to the issue of the day. Sánchez and his allies will be hoping that fact will not be lost on voters as the election campaign kicks off and as trade unions prepare a general strike over housing for 11 November.
Mindful, perhaps, of the distance between his words and his party’s voting history in congress, Feijóo called for people not to manipulate Abascal’s death to suit their own purposes.
“No campaigning, no political parties, no partisan ends, no more bricks in the wall,” he said on Wednesday night. “When a person dies there should be nothing but respect.”

blocks.caption: Migrants try to make their way past police officers in Ceuta after mass crossings on foot and by sea at the end of July from Morocco into Spanish territory. Photograph: Violeta Santos Moura/Reuters

blocks.text: And yet, despite the primacy of housing as an issue, Feijóo opted to start his campaign in Spain’s North African territory of Ceuta, where at least 141 people died as tens of thousands tried to cross over from neighbouring Morocco at the end of July. The Spanish government’s handling of the mass crossing, which saw about 80,000 people enter Ceuta, has been criticised at home and abroad. Speaking in the territory on Wednesday, Feijóo promised that its safety would be at the “top of [the] in-tray” if he became prime minister.

Vox, meanwhile, has responded to Absacal’s death by posting footage of a TV interview in which she said she held Sánchez responsible for what had happened to her. The far-right party accused the socialists of using “the suffering of an elderly person to stage a campaign to hide the government’s responsibility in the housing disaster”. It also suggested that Sánchez had visited “ruin and death” on Spain in the form of the floods that killed 230 people in Valencia two years ago, last year’s nationwide power cut, the deadly train crash in southern Spain in January, and recent events in Ceuta.

articles.title: Teacher who sexually abused pupil back in Indonesia jail after BBC investigation
articles.summary: Mochamad Subchi Azal Tsani had been secretly released on parole in 2025, after serving less than half his sentence.
articles.byline: Endang Nurdin and Rebecca Henschke, BBC News Indonesia

blocks.text: A former teacher who sexually assaulted a student has been returned to jail in Indonesia after a BBC investigation revealed he was secretly released early.

Mochamad Subchi Azal Tsani, known as Bechi, was sentenced to seven years in prison in 2022 after being convicted of sexually assaulting a female student at his father's prominent Islamic boarding school in East Java, where he worked as a teacher.

A BBC Eye undercover investigation revealed he was secretly released on parole in August 2025, after serving less than half his sentence. The woman he had been convicted of assaulting had not been informed - despite her legal right to know.
On hearing he was back in prison, she cried with relief.
"I pray that this doesn't happen to anyone else and that, going forward, the law will be applied justly in Indonesia," the former student, who wished to remain anonymous, told the BBC.
The Ministry of Immigration and Corrections previously told the BBC that Bechi was released because of sentence reductions granted in accordance with regulations.
But the BBC investigation sparked a public outcry and led to calls from lawmakers for an investigation, after which the government announced a comprehensive review.
That review found "errors" resulting in Bechi's parole being revoked. He has now been returned to prison.
Immigration and Corrections Minister Agus Andrianto told the BBC that those responsible for approving Bechi's parole "will certainly face sanctions".
"We want to make sure that such mistakes or irregularities do not happen again," he said.
For Ira Puspitasari, one of several former students who accused Bechi of sexual abuse and testified at his trial, the decision is a vindication.
"I'm amazed, really. I didn't expect the government would pay such detailed attention to this case and really pay attention to us, the victims," she said.
Ira, who has waived her legal right to anonymity, told the BBC she was raped and sexually abused by Bechi for more than four years, from the age of 15.
"I was treated as his slave. I was held captive, raped, beaten," she said.
She said she tried to run away but Bechi's private security guards tracked her down, kidnapped her and took her to a secluded hut, where Bechi tortured and raped her.

She said she reported all of this to the police but was then intimidated into withdrawing her complaint. She also shared an audio recording of Bechi's mother telling her to say that "nothing had happened".

articles.title: Russian attack on eastern Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk kills at least 33
articles.summary: A Russian bomb attack on the eastern Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk killed at least 33 people, authorities said Thursday, describing it as a targeted strike on ‌civilians in the key stronghold sought…

image.caption: A burning bus is shown following a Russian airstrike in the city of Kramatorsk, in Ukraine's Donetsk region, on Thursday. (Press service of the National Police of Ukraine/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

A Russian bomb attack on the eastern Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk killed at least 33 people, authorities said Thursday, describing it as a targeted strike on ‌civilians in the key stronghold sought by Moscow.
Ukrainian president says attack hit a bus stop

Another 18 people were wounded in one of the largest single attacks of this year, which took place on a street where two city ​buses were operating at the time, police said. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described it as a bus stop.
Images posted by police showed bodies strewn across a street littered with ​debris, as well as a charred shell of what appeared to ⁠be a bus.

"For ⁠them [the Russians], a bus with passengers ‌is an attractive target, precisely because one strike can kill as many people as possible," regional governor Vadym Filashkin said on the Telegram app.
Firefighters work at the site of a Russian airstrike, where a bus was hit in Kramatorsk on Thursday. (Press service of the State Emergency Service of Ukraine in Donetsk region/Reuters)
There was no immediate comment from Moscow on the attack.
Russia denies ⁠targeting civilians, though it has regularly pounded Ukrainian cities, towns and other targets during its full-scale invasion that began in February 2022.
Intensifying strikes on cities
Moscow's forces have stepped ‌up drone and guided-bomb strikes on Kramatorsk and other cities in Ukraine's "fortress belt," local officials say, the backbone of its defences in the Donetsk region.

Russia has demanded that Ukraine cede the rest of the region still ​under its control before it stops fighting, which Kyiv refuses to do. The pace of Moscow's battlefield ⁠gains in the region has significantly slowed this year.

items: Russian strike devastates apartment block in northern Ukraine, at least 25 killed across the country
Russia to intensify strikes on Ukraine after Zelenskyy remarks, defence ministry says

blocks.text: Filashkin said he had ordered ⁠city authorities in Kramatorsk and Sloviansk, another key fortress-belt city, to halt ⁠public transport, ⁠saying "we have no right to ​risk" citizens' lives.
Thursday's attack came a day after dozens were killed in a massive ​Russian air attack ⁠across Ukraine, primarily targeting the country's power grid.

Separately on Thursday, three people were killed and 14 wounded in morning drone strikes on the capital of Kyiv, said Mayor Vitali Klitschko. Russian forces have unleashed frequent waves of attacks on Kyiv amid a shortage of ⁠Ukrainian air defences.

articles.title: Racial and religious hate crimes at record high in England and Wales, data shows
articles.summary: Offences targeting Muslims increased most in 12 months to March – up 15% – while antisemitic hate crimes rose by 10%

blocks.text: Racially and religiously motivated offences have reached record highs in the UK, as the government’s main Islamophobia partner says attacks on mosques are increasing in severity.

New Home Office figures show police recorded 146,825 hate crimes in the year ending March 2026 – a rise of 7% in the past year. Offences targeting Muslims increased the most – up 15%, from 4,479 to 5,132 – while antisemitic hate crimes rose by 10%, from 2,874 to 3,162.
The data excluded figures for the Metropolitan police because of a change in their crime recording system.
Religious hate crime offences recorded in England and Wales in the 12 months to March – excluding the Met – were at their highest annual total – 8,214 – since records began in 2012.
The Home Office reported sharp increases in anti-Muslim offences in September 2025, coinciding with protests and public disorder, and again in March after the outbreak of war between the US and Iran.
Anti-Muslim hate crimes reached a record 3,660 offences, the highest annual total since this data was first collected in 2018.

The official data comes as The British Muslim Trust (BMT), appointed by the government in July 2025 to monitor anti-Muslim hostility, said there had been a shift from hate aimed at mosques to “targeting [the] Muslims inside”.
BMT recorded 78 incidents involving 64 mosques across the UK and the Channel Islands between 21 July 2025 and 30 July 2026, roughly equivalent to an incident every five days.

A report published on Thursday by BMT, titled A Year of Division, said: “There has been an unprecedented level of anti-Muslim hate during the last year … The momentum of growing anti-Muslim hostility is driving the attacks against mosques … The defining shift across this reporting period is a movement from hate aimed at the mosque itself to hate targeting Muslims inside it.”

blocks.caption: Supporters of Ukip march in London. Photograph: Martin Pope/Getty Images

blocks.text: According to BMT’s own seven-level severity scale, 62.7% of incidents since November 2025 fell into the upper four levels – threats and sustained harassment; weapon present or threats to kill; arson or direct violence; and alleged mass-casualty plots. Between July and October 2025, just 22.2% of incidents were of the more serious kind.
BMT added: “Political figures and commentators should take greater care when raising policy concerns regarding immigration or integration.
“Rhetoric intended as policy critique on immigration or integration can often become incendiary and difficult to distinguish from hostility directed at British Muslim communities specifically.”

Ammer Amin, trustee of Masjid Al-Ummah, a planned mosque on the site of a former church in Watford, which has been repeatedly targeted, said: “It’s almost open season [on Muslims] and people feel emboldened by politicians.

“It’s easy to say it’s the Reform party, but it’s not just the Reform party. It’s the Conservative party as well. I’m not party political, but they’re singing from the same hymn sheet. They’re almost competing.”

Amin said the mosque’s plans included a sports hall, gym, nursery and food bank for the use of everyone in the local community. In October last year, crucifixes were sprayed on the building’s hoardings. A man later admitted possession of a knife and an axe, but was cleared of criminal damage. In February this year, model pigs were thrown into the premises in another incident.

Akeela Ahmed, BMT’s CEO, said: “Security needs are increasing … and many Muslims today are scared to go about their everyday lives. We need to reduce the need for protection and address the root causes of hate against Muslim communities.”
Meanwhile, the Community Security Trust has said “antisemitic hate crime remains at an unacceptably high level”.
The new government data showed hate crimes against Jewish people were, when data from the Met was excluded, at their second highest level on record.
A total of 2,003 offences were recorded, just below the peak of 2,093 in the year ending March 2024, which followed the 7 October Hamas attacks on Israel and the subsequent war in Gaza.

articles.title: Italy overhauls electoral system after fiercely contested debate
articles.summary: Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni says the move will deliver more stable government, but opposition parties say her aim is to stay in power.

blocks.text: Italy's parliament has approved fiercely contested changes to the country's electoral system championed by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni ahead of elections due next year.
Lawmakers voted 227 to 164 in favour of moving to a fully proportional system, which Meloni has argued will boost the chance of clear winners and more stable government.
Opposition parties say her right-wing coalition has designed the proposals to improve its chance of retaining power and, in a heated debate on Thursday, accused it of flouting democracy.
Meloni had warned she could resign and trigger an early election if the plans were rejected, with the secret ballot seen as a test of her authority.
Meloni's coalition has overseen a rare period of political stability for Italy since her election in 2022, and last month her government became the country's longest-running since World War Two.

The voting reform will see the country move away from its current hybrid voting system, in which about a third of members are chosen through a first-past-the-post vote and the rest through proportional representation.
Parties proposing to form a coalition will be required to put forward their joint candidate for prime minister, and their political programme, before any general election.
A coalition or party winning more than 42% of the vote will be awarded dozens of additional seats in parliament - which could turn a narrow victory into a more comfortable majority.
In a debate ahead of the vote, centre-left members accused the government of forcing through the new voting rules.
"Go ahead and change the electoral law, we will win in any case under any voting system," said Democratic Party (PD) leader Elly Schlein.

articles.title: Royal Navy member appears in court charged with spying for Russia
articles.summary:
Teddy Young, 24, from Bedfordshire, accused of drafting a message in Russian containing classified information

A serving member of the Royal Navy has appeared in court charged with spying…

blocks.text: A serving member of the Royal Navy has appeared in court charged with spying for Russia.

Teddy Young, 24, was accused of obtaining protected information that could benefit an unnamed foreign power. He was arrested at his home in Bedfordshire on Tuesday after an investigation by Counter Terrorism Policing London (CTPL).
He had been charged with offences under the National Security Act, the Metropolitan police said on Thursday.
Young, a naval intelligence rating, is alleged to have abused high-level security clearance to access secret defence and intelligence data after being deployed on a navy vessel.
He is accused of drafting a message in Russian containing classified information and had allegedly taken steps to make direct contact with the Russian authorities.
Young was first arrested in May last year. At that point he was suspended and relieved of his duties, and he was on gardening leave until his latest arrest.
Young appeared at Westminster magistrates court wearing a grey navy tracksuit, and he spoke only to confirm his name.

While there was no application for bail, the district judge Annabelle Pilling told Young: “On the basis of the information I have already read, there are substantial grounds to believe that if granted bail you would not come back to court and that you would make efforts to avoid further court appearances and would commit further offences.”
Young was remanded in custody to appear before a specialist judge at the Old Bailey on 16 October.

The Crown Prosecution Service authorised the charges on Wednesday. They allege that between 26 November 2024 and 21 May 2025 Young engaged in conduct in preparation for committing an offence of disclosing protected information.
It is also alleged that in the same period he obtained, copied, recorded or retained protected information, intending the conduct to benefit a foreign power.

Commander Helen Flanagan, the head of CTPL, said in a statement issued before the court appearance: “These are very serious charges against a serving member of the armed forces. We have worked extremely closely with relevant operational colleagues within the Ministry of Defence as our investigation has progressed to ensure appropriate measures could be taken to mitigate any potential risks linked to this matter.”
The arrest and charges are not connected to the recent investigation into an incident at RAF Fairford.

A Royal Navy spokesperson said: “A member of the Royal Navy has been charged with National Security Act offences following an investigation by Counter Terrorism Policing London. As legal proceedings are ongoing, it would be inappropriate to comment further at this stage.”

articles.title: Bear kills man in home attack near Mongolian capital
articles.summary: Police say the bear entered a traditional nomadic dwelling near Ulaanbaatar, killing a man and seriously injured a woman.

blocks.text: A bear has killed a man and seriously injured a woman after it attacked them in their home near the Mongolian capital, Ulaanbaatar.
Police say the incident happened in the Bayanzurkh district overnight on Wednesday in their traditional Mongolian nomadic tent-like structure known as a ger.

The man, who was in his 40s, died, but the woman, in her 50s, managed to flee and raise the alarm with neighbours. She is in a serious condition in hospital, city official Munkhbayar M told reporters.
Sightings of bears around humans are becoming more common in Mongolia, for reasons that include climate change and food scarcity.
A team of rangers is searching for the bear while officials have warned locals to be vigilant and report any sightings.
There had been 24 bear sightings near the capital this year alone, compared to just two in 2018, Munkhbayar said, in comments reported by the AFP news agency.

Videos showing bears entering or damaging gers, and attacking livestock have reportedly gone viral on Mongolian social media in recent weeks, highlighting the increase in bear and human interaction across the country.
Bear-hunting permits across eight provinces have been issued and officials are seeking to obtain tranquiliser dart guns to support rangers in rural areas, AFP reports.
A significant amount of Mongolians are nomadic, but settled agricultural communities are becoming more common. An increasing number of the population lives in the capital or other major urban areas.

articles.title: Security in the Black Sea region: is Bulgaria the weak link in Europe's defense against threats from Russia?
articles.summary: Two ships have sunk off the coast of Bulgaria and Romania after drone attacks in recent days. Sofia has held back on pointing the finger at Russia. What does that mean for security in the Black Sea…

image.caption: A Bulgarian border police vessel carries crew members from a ship damaged in a drone attack on TuesdayImage: Petko Momchilov/REUTERS

blocks.text: Although security in the Baltic Sea and the threat of Russian provocation there are the subject of regular public debate, security in the Black Sea is a subject that sometimes gets less attention in the context of Russia's war in Ukraine even though the Black Sea is to a degree an active frontline in the war.
There are multiple reasons why the Black Sea's security is such a complex issue, but two incidents in recent days have highlighted just how precarious the situation there is.
On October 6, two cargo ships — the Alfa Watan and the Able — were struck by drones in the Bulgarian exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea.
The Alfa Watan sank, and its crew has not been recovered. Bulgaria conducted a search and rescue operation, which was called off on Wednesday morning.
The crew of the Able, which was damaged, was rescued by a passing Bulgarian ship. Two crew members were taken to the military hospital in Varna.

blocks.caption: Crew members from a ship damaged in a drone attack disembark from a Bulgarian border police vessel on TuesdayImage: Petko Momchilov/REUTERS

blocks.text: The day before, another cargo ship — the Royad Mammadov — was struck by a drone and sank off the coast of Romania. Two crew members lost their lives.
Multiple recent attacks on ships
These are not isolated incidents. In the past few months there have been multiple attacks on cargo ships carrying grain from Ukraine.
As a result, doubt is increasingly being cast on the belief that the western part of the Black Sea — the area off the coast of Bulgaria and Romania — is relatively safe.

"Тhe Black Sea front is clearly expanding, and we should no longer look only to the Baltic Sea as a potential avenue for escalation and aggressive actions," said Ruslan Trad, global security expert and non-resident fellow at the Atlantic Council's Digital Forensic Research Lab.
PM downplays drone attacks

Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev downplayed the attack on the ships, remarking that ships are constantly being sunk in the Black Sea and that Tuesday's drone attacks were "probably not the most serious incident."
Bulgaria's government called Tuesday's attack on the two vessels an "absolutely unacceptable violation of international law" but refrained from calling on Russia to end its war against Ukraine.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, on the other hand, was unequivocal. He said that the Ukrainian military had assured Bulgaria that it was not responsible for the attack and pointed the finger squarely at Russia.
After a meeting of the National Security Council on Wednesday, a declaration was issued, which once again did not name the source of the threat in the Black Sea.

Radev stated that the cargo and the direction of travel of the ships "logically speaking" provide grounds for a hypothesis pointing to Russia but stressed that there is no concrete evidence. He also contradicted Zelenskyy, saying no such conversation had taken place.
Earlier he said that "if the war is not brought to an end in due time, it will continue to expand."
Similarly, Bulgaria's Foreign Minister Velislava Petrova said that "we need to support all possible diplomatic efforts to bring this war to an end."

blocks.caption: Bulgarian PM Rumen Radev said that there is no concrete evidence that Russia was behind the attackImage: Spasiyana Sergieva/REUTERS

blocks.text: The refusal to state clearly that it is Russian aggression that is putting the region at risk is not new for the Radev administration.
Is Bulgaria a 'weak link' in European defense?

For Rumena Filipova, chairperson of the Institute of Global Analytics, this is an example of how Bulgaria seems to be a weak link in Europe's defense against malicious influence from Russia and China.
"This weakness stems from the lack of a serious institutional response to hybrid attacks of any kind, the absence of appropriate measures and a general tendency to downplay incidents," she told DW.

"The perpetrator is not named explicitly, even though our partners in the European Union and NATO have already issued numerous warnings about what aggressive steps Russia could take against Europe," she said.

According to Filipova, the Bulgarian government's narrative about peace without actually specifying the conditions or consequences for Ukrainian and European security is a demonstration of its leniency toward Moscow and raises the question of Sofia's geopolitical orientation.
No smoking gun
One of the surviving members of the Able's crew has said that he believes it was a Russian strike because the ship was carrying Ukrainian grain.

blocks.caption: The cargo vessel Able (pictured here in Istanbul, Turkey, on an unknown date), which was carrying Ukrainian grain, was damaged when hit by a drone on October 6Image: Tony Hogwood/REUTERS

blocks.text: Ruslan Trad says that the crew member's testimony is an eyewitness hypothesis, not hard proof.

"The logic of motive, however, points toward Russia, as it is the state systematically threatening navigation to Ukrainian ports," he told DW, adding, "Until more concrete data is revealed the most accurate phrasing is 'probable but unproven Russian responsibility' without excluding other possibilities."

Trad also pointed out that Bulgarian institutions lack experience in attributing maritime drones in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone (EEZ). "When the system is uncertain, the safest institutional reaction is to say nothing until certainty is achieved," he said. "That is caution, but it is also a political choice."
Economic consequences
A direct military response or the triggering of NATO's Article 5, which guarantees collective defense in the event of an attack on any member state, should not be expected.

blocks.caption: A marine drone, which Romanian Defense Minister Radu Miruta said was destroyed by F-16 fighter jets in AugustImage: Radu Miruta via Facebook/Handout/REUTERS

blocks.text: Bulgaria's EEZ in the Black Sea is not Bulgarian sovereign territory and, as such, the strikes on the ships in this zone do not constitute a direct attack on Bulgaria — or on Romania in the case of the Royad Mammadov.
Nevertheless, Ruslan Trad thinks these three incidents shatter the illusion that the western part of the Black Sea is a safe zone because of the distance between it and the frontlines in Ukraine.
"This will increase pressure for tighter maritime monitoring, anti‑mining capabilities, coordination between coastal guard services and intelligence‑sharing among allies," he said.

"The real effect will be a hardening of the shipping regime: stricter routing recommendations, higher insurance premiums and more difficulty hiring crews. Economic repercussions for local businesses can also be anticipated — imagine the impact on fishermen if they have to stay in ports constantly due to fear of further attacks. That is the intended effect of such strikes," he added.
Rumena Filipova believes that although Romania, Bulgaria and Turkey strengthened their Mine Countermeasures Black Sea Task Group at this year's NATO summit in Ankara, this is not enough.

She says there are far more substantial gaps in naval defense capabilities: "Modernization of Bulgaria's naval forces must be improved, much greater coordination — especially with Romania — is required. Yet, for more than a decade, Bulgarian authorities have downplayed or ignored the idea of developing joint naval defense forces and coordination, and that trend continues today," she said.
Turkey's leverage and China's role

Another question is how Turkey will react to recent developments. All three ships were owned by Turkish firms and some of the crew members were Turkish nationals. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan on Wednesday spoke to Russian President Vladimir Putin about the security of navigation in the Black Sea.

blocks.caption: Another cargo ship, the Royad Mammadov, was struck by a drone and sank off the coast of Romania on October 5. Pictured here: Firefighters and rescue workers wait to help the survivorsImage: Romanian Interior Ministry/Handout/REUTERS

blocks.text: Trad notes that Ankara has several levers of influence in the Black Sea: control of the Straits under the Montreux Convention, the largest fleet in the Black Sea and its role as a mediator between Moscow and Kyiv.

"A realistic scenario is intensified diplomacy, coordination with Bucharest and Sofia, and pressure for safe navigation, probably within the existing trilateral anti‑mining cooperation. If it turns out that Turkish citizens were killed in a deliberate attack, Ankara's stance could become markedly tougher," he said.
Filipova thinks that Black Sea security is already being perceived as a core issue — not only for the region but for NATO as a whole.

In her view, there's not enough coordination between the countries in the region, which means that any response to threats does not come from a united front — something she feels has to change urgently.
Filipova says that China's influence in the region and how it's connected with Russia is another factor.

"We see not only the concrete military threat from Russia but also a subtler threat from China, which is less publicly discussed. But Beijing is trying to acquire strategic assets in ports, thereby gaining influence over both trade and critical infrastructure," she said. "Given that China and Russia cooperate closely, this constitutes a double threat for the Black Sea region."

articles.title: Anne Carson wins Nobel prize in literature 2026
articles.summary:
World’s most prestigious prize for literature goes to Canadian poet known for genre-crossing works including Autobiography of Red

The Nobel prize in literature has been awarded to the…

blocks.text: The Nobel prize in literature has been awarded to the Canadian poet and essayist Anne Carson, the Swedish Academy has announced.
The academy cited the author’s “bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature”.
Born in 1950 in Toronto, Carson is known for work that moves freely between poetry, prose and translation, drawing heavily on the literature and mythology of the ancient Greek world.
Carson’s first book, Eros the Bittersweet, was published in 1986, and combined literary criticism with an exploration of desire and the ancient Greek tradition.

Her best-known work is Autobiography of Red, a 1998 novel in verse inspired by the fragments of the ancient Greek poet Stesichorus. It reimagines the myth of Geryon, the red-winged monster killed by Herakles, as the story of a modern teenage boy navigating heartbreak and desire.
In 2001, she became the first woman to win the TS Eliot prize for her collection The Beauty of the Husband. She has also been awarded Guggenheim and MacArthur fellowships.

Her work has attracted praise from fellow writers, including Susan Sontag, who once said: “She is one of the few writers writing in English that I would read anything she wrote. If there’s a magazine that has something of hers in it, I buy it automatically.”

Carson’s books have ranged widely in form. Men in the Off Hours combined verse essays, poems, epitaphs and prose about artists and historical figures, and won the inaugural Griffin poetry prize in 2001. Decreation, another eclectic work, brought together poetry, essays and an opera. Nox, published in 2010, is particularly characteristic of Carson’s avante-garde approach to literature – the book takes the form of an accordion-fold box containing a reproduction of a notebook Carson made after the death of her brother. Her later works include Red Doc> and Float.

The Nobel prize in literature has been awarded on 118 previous occasions since 1901. Recent laureates include Annie Ernaux, Bob Dylan, Abdulrazak Gurnah, Louise Glück, Peter Handke and Olga Tokarczuk. Last year’s recipient was the Hungarian author László Krasznahorkai, known for his dystopic and avant-garde writing.
Carson, 76, will formally receive the medal and diploma in a ceremony in Stockholm in December.

articles.title: French police arrest 5 suspects over Renoir museum theft
articles.summary: Thieves broke into the Renoir Museum on the French Riviera last month and made off with two paintings. The heist follows a string of high-profile robberies from European museums.

image.caption: The robbers escaped with two paintings from the Renoir Museum after fleeing from policeImage: Valery Hache/AFP

blocks.text: French police have arrested at least five suspects in connection with the theft of two Renoir paintings from a museum in southern France last month, local media reported.

Two burglars cut through a fence and smashed a window to enter the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer on September 8. They then used an electric saw to cut through the frame mountings, according to the local mayor.

The thieves initially took four Renoir artworks, valued together at around €9 million ($10.5 million), but dropped two in the museum's garden as they fled from police who had been alerted by the alarm system.
The daily Nice Martin newspaper, which first broke the news of the arrests, said six people were taken into custody, including the two suspected burglars.
Prosecutors in Marseille, who are leading the investigation, declined to comment.

blocks.caption: The Renoir Museum is housed in the last home of French Impressionist painter Pierre-Auguste RenoirImage: Johanna Hoelzl/picture alliance

blocks.text: What happened to the artworks?
The two paintings stolen from the museum were the Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano (1910) and Jeune fille au puits (1886).
Nice Martin reported that the whereabouts of the artworks was not immediately known.

Founded in 1960, the Renoir Museum is located in the former home and studio of French Impressionist painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir on the Cote d'Azur. The property houses 12 of his artworks and is surrounded by gardens and olive trees.
The heist in Cagnes-sur-Mer was the latest in a series of museum robberies, including the daylight theft of the French crown jewels from the Louvre Museum in Paris last year.
Four suspects have been arrested over that case, but the jewels they are accused of taking, with a value of around $100 million, have not been recovered.

articles.title: How a multibillion-dollar oilfield has ignited UK-Argentina feud over the Falklands
articles.summary: Argentina and the UK once fought a war over the Falkland Islands. Now the multibillion-dollar Sea Lion oil project has reignited old tensions, with Buenos Aires seeking to put a stop to the plans.

image.caption: A huge underwater oil project could transform the Falkland Islands' economy, but it is also fueling a sovereignty dispute between Argentina and the UKImage: Martin Zwick/Danita Delimont/IMAGO

blocks.text: Home to less than 4,000 people and located in an isolated corner of the South Atlantic Ocean, the Falkland Islands don't often feature in global business headlines.
However, a UK-Israeli oil exploration project in its waters is stoking long-running tensions between Argentina and the people of the archipelago.

Argentina has laid claim to the islands for two centuries and refers to them as Las Malvinas. This 200-year-old dispute over the islands' sovereignty led to a 1982 war between the UK and Argentina, though British control was quickly restored after Argentine forces invaded the islands.

A 2013 sovereignty referendum on the islands returned a 99.8% vote in favor of remaining tied to the UK as a self-governing British Overseas Territory. Now the Sea Lion oilfield project has brought the issue back to the surface.
Last month, Argentine President Javier Milei threatened to launch an international legal challenge against the UK unless the project is stopped within two weeks.

The oil project is being operated by Israeli company Navitas Petroleum and the UK's Rockhopper Exploration and has the full support of the Falkand Islands Legislative Assembly, which has pursued the project since 2010. The companies plan to begin extracting oil from the Sea Lion oilfield by early 2028.

Milei says the project is "the illegal plundering of our resources" and that he will take the matter to the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea, an independent judicial body responsible for the application of the United Nations' Convention on the Law of the Sea.
Rally around the flag?

Stacy Bragger, a member of the Falklands Islands' 12-member assembly, told DW that the dispute was "nothing new" and that Argentina is using the oil project as "a vehicle to pursue their sovereignty claim."
He thinks Milei may be stepping up rhetoric ahead of the 2027 elections in Argentina.
"When there's elections coming up, the Falklands is a very convenient tool to use in order to rally people together and distract them from domestic problems," he said.

blocks.caption: Stacy Bragger, a member of the Falkand Islands' Legislative AssemblyImage: Legislative Assembly of the Falkland Islands

blocks.text: Henry Ziemer, an analyst with the Americas program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington, says the Falklands is "a perennial sore spot in Argentine politics" and that since the 1980s, various governments have raised the issue in an attempt to rally support and to "stoke the fires of nationalism."

He thinks Milei's intervention is noteworthy given that he had previously been open to better relations with the UK on the issue. He agrees that it may be a strategy to "boost approval ratings at a time when the government is under a lot of strong domestic pressure."
Potentially transformative for the Falklands
Even if Milei sees political gain in the issue, the possibility of the Sea Lion project being successful would significantly raise the economic stakes for all concerned.

The project has a budget of $1.8 billion (€1.6 billion) and could generate revenues of more than double that for the Falkland Islands. The companies hope that at its peak, the field will produce up to 50,000 barrels per day and could last for up to 35 years.

That would substantially increase the Falklands' current annual GDP, which is almost entirely dependent on the volatile fishing sector and tourism. The administration is even looking into the possibility of creating a sovereign wealth fund if the oil project is successful.

"It's a very significant project for us with a lot of potential for our future," said Bragger. "It's been a big effort to get to this point and assuming all goes to plan, we want to retain as much value as possible."
However, beyond playing to domestic politics, Milei may also spy an opportunity for Argentina to position itself as an energy player amid the war in Iran and the troubles in the Strait of Hormuz.

blocks.caption: Argentina's President Javier Milei says he is taking legal action against the Sea Lion oilfield projectImage: Argentina's Presidency Press Office/AFP

blocks.text: Argentina's own domestic oil sector is growing, with production surging at Patagonia's Vaca Muerta, one of the world's largest shale developments. Were his legal efforts to prove successful, there may be further gains.
"When natural resources overlay existing territorial disputes and bad blood, that tends to galvanize a lot of conflict," said Ziemer.
However, Bragger counters that Milei and Argentina have no legitimate claim to either the Falklands or whatever oil wealth may be extracted over the coming years.
"They don't respect our right to self-determination," he added. "They don't respect our right to develop our own resources. They just want to colonize us."
More economic pressure from Argentina

Milei plans to put pressure on the Falklands by stepping up existing economic sanctions. Andrea Clausen, chief executive of the Falklands since 2025, recently described this campaign as "economic warfare."

Many international suppliers and shipping companies already refuse to supply the Falklands for fear of angering Argentina. Now, Milei's government has initiated sanctions against 60 people involved in the Sea Lion project.

blocks.caption: The project could transform the Falklands' small economyImage: Ashley Cooper/Pond5 Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: In a televised address last month, he also vowed to sanction the companies involved in the project. Such a move could cast doubt on the project, which previously collapsed in 2014 and 2020, due to financing troubles, oil-price weakness and delays caused by sanctions.

Navitas this week confirmed that two contractors had pulled out of the project due to sanctions concerns and that it was replacing them. There are also concerns that Milei could try to garner international support in favor of his position, with President Donald Trump recently suggesting that US support for the status quo on the islands was "under review."

Bragger plays this down, pointing to recent comments from US Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirming support for the Falklands. Ziemer says it would be "very shocking" if the United States came down on the side of Argentina.
While uncertainty reigns over whether the oil project ultimately gets going or not, there is little expectation that the dispute could lead to a return of armed conflict like in 1982.
"That's a step too far, and the situation would have to dramatically deteriorate before we would see the potential for military conflict," said Ziemer.

articles.title: Overwatch season 5 adds new hero, map and major changes
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Blizzard Entertainment released Overwatch Season 5, “A Grim Doctrine,” on October 7, opening the final chapter of the game’s Reign of Talon storyline with new gameplay content,…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Blizzard Entertainment released Overwatch Season 5, “A Grim Doctrine,” on October 7, opening the final chapter of the game’s Reign of Talon storyline with new gameplay content, seasonal events and major hero changes.
The update introduces Doctrine, a new Support hero with a violent history tied to Doomfist, after the latter breaks him out of Grímsvötn prison.
Doctrine’s kit includes an Eternal Scepter that heals allies and damages enemies at mid-to-long range, while bat-like drones boost the team’s healing and attack speed.
His Ultimate redistributes lifeforce across the battlefield, giving allies Overhealth while reducing enemy health.

Grímsvötn also joins the game as the first new Escort map in years. Set inside a Talon-controlled prison built into an Icelandic volcanic fissure, the map expands the season’s Reign of Talon storyline.
RELATED STORY: Monster Hunter Outlanders launches globally on October 29
Halloween event and crossover

The Halloween event, Mystery Madness: Graveyard Games, began October 7 and runs through November 2 (AEDT). Players respawn with random powers after each death, while weekly votes determine whether Ashe, Moira or Winston is summoned next. The mode’s roster eventually expands to 20 heroes.

The season also features an Overwatch x Shadow Monarch crossover running through October 20 (AEDT), bringing anime-inspired skins based on the series to five heroes: Genji as Sung Jinwoo, Reaper as Igris, Anran as Cha Hae-In, Reinhardt as Iron, and Lifeweaver as Choi Jong-In.
Hero changes and rewards

One of the season’s biggest gameplay changes is Sombra’s move from the Damage role to Support. Blizzard described the change as one of its biggest alterations to an existing hero. Roadhog also received a rework that changes his Scrap Gun and adds a new Trash Compactor ability.

The update brings back Unvaulted Passes, allowing players to earn rewards from revised Battle Passes from Seasons 1 through 15. It also introduces two new Mythics: Dragon Shaoxia Wuyang and Lucio’s first Mythic Weapon, Treblemaker.

Halloween-themed Battle Pass skins arrive with the season, followed by the Tech Witches cosmetic collection from October. 10 to 26 (AEDT). Competitive Team Drives return in October. 30 to 31 (AEDT), leading into the Reign of Talon finale.

articles.title: Senate ratifies Philippines-France visiting forces agreement
articles.summary: The Senate on Thursday approved on third and final reading a resolution concurring in the ratification of the defense agreement between the Philippines and France that will provide a legal framework…

blocks.text: Published October 8, 2026 7:37pm

The Senate on Thursday approved on third and final reading a resolution concurring in the ratification of the defense agreement between the Philippines and France that will provide a legal framework for visiting military forces from both countries.

Senate Resolution No. 650, which concurs in the ratification of the Status of Visiting Forces Agreement (SOVFA) between the Philippines and France, was approved with 17 affirmative votes, with no negative votes or abstentions.

France will become the first European country to have a visiting forces agreement with the Philippines, joining the United States, Australia, Japan, Canada, and New Zealand as countries with defense access arrangements with Manila.

The PH-France SOVFA is a reciprocal agreement that establishes the legal framework governing the presence and activities of the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) and French Armed Forces, including their respective civilian components, in each other’s territories.
It also facilitates joint defense activities, military training, humanitarian operations, and other activities mutually agreed upon by the two countries.

The agreement seeks to boost the operational readiness and interoperability of the two countries’ armed forces “by facilitating the timely movement of personnel and resources and strengthening their capacity to coordinate and respond to security challenges, crises, and emergencies.”

“Next year, we will be celebrating 80 years of bilateral ties with France. Let our concurrence be a symbolic step towards a strengthened friendship with France and the European Union, and a concrete step forward towards stronger defense capabilities for the Philippines,” Senate Majority Leader Juan Miguel Zubiri, the measure’s author, said.
“As political conflicts continue to divide the world, it becomes more important that we form stronger alliances and ties with like-minded democracies such as France,” he added.
The Department of National Defense (DND) welcomed the Senate’s approval, describing France as a reliable Philippine partner in upholding international law.

“France has been one of the reliable partners of the Philippines in upholding international law. As a maritime power, it is a state party to the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) and has consistently articulated support for and recognition of the 2016 Arbitral Award,” the DND said.
The agency also highlighted France’s advanced defense capabilities, saying these could support the Philippines’ efforts to strengthen its defense supply chains.
“France's consistent willingness to not only participate but also grow convergence across our shared domains makes it an indispensable partner of the Philippines,” the DND added.

The DND said it would continue to deepen defense cooperation with like-minded countries to strengthen the Philippines’ deterrent capabilities and support regional and global resilience against actions that undermine the rules-based international order.

The 1987 Constitution prohibits foreign troops from establishing permanent military bases in the Philippines. Visiting forces agreements, however, provide a legal framework for the temporary presence of foreign military personnel for activities agreed upon by the countries involved.

The Philippines and the United States have a VFA that took effect in 1999, providing the legal framework for the temporary presence of US forces in the country for military exercises and humanitarian and disaster-response activities.
The Philippines also signed a similar agreement with Australia in 2007.
In April 2025, the Philippines and New Zealand signed their SOVFA. — VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Residents airlifted to safety after flooding in central Chile
articles.summary: The Mapocho river has burst its banks after an unusually large amount of rain fell in recent days.

blocks.text: Police in central Chile have airlifted several residents to safety after rising floodwaters left them trapped in their homes.
Recent torrential rains caused the Mapocho river to burst its banks, flooding large parts of the city of Talagante, 35km (22 miles) south-west of the capital, Santiago.
Santiago has seen 74mm of rainfall in the first seven days of this month, making it the rainiest October for the area in 76 years, meteorologists have said.

They have warned that this year's unusually strong El Niño climate phenomenon will likely continue to bring unusually wet weather, powerful winds and storms to the region during the southern hemisphere's spring.
Officials said one person had been found dead in a flooded underpass in the city of San Bernardo, south of Santiago, although they have yet to confirm the cause of death.
In Talagante, police used helicopters to rescue people and pets living on the banks of the Mapocho who had been surprised by the fast-rising waters overnight.
Dirt roads turned into rivers in the riverside community which, unlike in July's storms, had not been evacuated ahead of the heavy downpours.

articles.title: Canadian writer Anne Carson wins 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature
articles.summary: The Canadian poet and essayist's work often blends verse, prose, dialogue, and translation in a genre-defying mix

blocks.text: NOBEL LAUREATE. Copies of books by Anne Carson, winner of the 2026 Nobel Prize for Literature, are displayed at Waterstones bookshop in London, Britain, on October 8, 2026.
Hannah McKay/Reuters
The Canadian poet and essayist's work often blends verse, prose, dialogue, and translation in a genre-defying mix

items: Anne Carson, a Canadian poet and writer, won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature for her innovative work that engages with classical traditions.
The prize, awarded by the Swedish Academy, is valued at 12 million Swedish crowns ($1.2 million) and recognizes Carson's genre-defying blend of verse, prose, and translation.

Carson's notable works include translations of classical Greek literature and the performance piece 'Norma Jeane Baker of Troy,' placing her among esteemed past laureates like Alexander Solzhenitsyn and Alice Munro.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

STOCKHOLM, Sweden – Canadian poet and writer Anne Carson won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature “for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature,” the award-giving body said on Thursday, October 8.
The prize is awarded by the Swedish Academy and is worth 12 million Swedish crowns ($1.2 million).
Canadian poet and essayist Carson’s work often blends verse, prose, dialogue and translation in a genre-defying mix.

She is widely known for her translations of classical Greek literature, which heavily influence her work, which ranges from opera libretti to literary criticism and verse novels such as “Autobiography of Red” from 1998.
Her style is exemplified in “Norma Jeane Baker of Troy” from 2019, a performance piece which mixes the stories of Helen of Troy in Euripides’ play “Helen” and Marilyn Monroe.
Carson takes a place beside luminaries such as Alexander Solzhenitsyn, Alice Munro and Ernest Hemingway as a recipient of the award, which often divides opinion among book lovers.

The Academy has been lambasted for ignoring some of the literary titans of the last 120 years such as Leo Tolstoy, Virginia Woolf and Jorge Luis Borges, criticised for snubbing US authors — though it gave the prize to singer-songwriter Bob Dylan in 2016 — and accused of being too obscure in its choices.

Defenders say the Academy has made popular picks, such as Colombia’s Gabriel Garcia Marquez in 1982 and Doris Lessing in 2007, arguing that part of its task is to highlight lesser-known literary traditions and encourage readers to broaden their horizons.
Established in the will of Swedish dynamite inventor and businessman Alfred Nobel, the prizes for achievements in literature, science and peace have been awarded since 1901.
Last year’s prize was won by Hungarian writer Laszlo Krasznahorkai, dubbed the “master of the apocalypse” by American critic Susan Sontag. – Rappler.com
