articles.title: Gov't aid amid El Niño might be too late for beneficiaries, says farmers' group
articles.summary: A farmers" group said on Thursday that the government"s response to a potentially strong El Niño could be already late for its intended beneficiaries.

blocks.text: Published October 8, 2026 3:46pm
A farmers’ group said on Thursday that the government’s response to a potentially strong El Niño could be already late for its intended beneficiaries.
The Federation of Free Farmers Cooperatives, Inc. (FFCI) said that planned subsidies for farmers should be given in cash instead as the government action might take time to arrive.
“Itong El Niño, last year pa pinag uusapan na nila. Ngayon pa lang sila gumagalaw,” said FFFCI National Manager Raul Montemayor in an interview with Super Radyo dzBB.
(They have been talking about El Niño since last year. They are only taking action now.)

“Kaya ako naiisip ko, huwag na ‘yung mga subsidy, ibigay na lang ng pera, kung ano mang pera ang available at ibigay sa mga magsasaka. Hayaan na lang ang mga magsasaka na mag diskarte. Kung ano yung kailangan nilang gawin…bahala sila na gamitin, kaysa maghintay sa gobyerno.”

(That's why I think, forget about the subsidies—just give them cash, whatever money is available, and release it to the farmers. Let the farmers figure out how to manage it themselves. Whatever they need to do… leave it to them on how to use it, rather than waiting for the government.)
“By the time na maibigay sa kanila ‘yung mga ayuda, abono, fuel subsidy, tapos na yung El Niño,” Montemayor further said.
(By the time the financial aid, fertilizers, and fuel subsidies are actually distributed to them, El Niño will already be over.)
GMA News Online reached out to the Department of Agriculture (DA) for comment.
The DA earlier said that it sought P45 billion funding to assist farmers and fisherfolk in the looming prolonged drought, which is expected to persist until early 2027.
The request will cover fuel subsidies to farmers and fisherfolk in areas affected by the Habagat and those that experienced drought in the past, mostly in Luzon.

The DA said that it has already begun releasing fuel assistance to registered fisherfolk this week. While mechanized farmers could start receiving the subsidy by the last week of October or in November.
There are 106 areas in the country so far that have already declared a state of calamity due to El Niño. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: DOJ: Vigilance, looking for patterns could prevent potential school violence
articles.summary: "Nag-a-announce muna, eh. Kaya sinabi ko maging mapagmatyag. Si Kuya, si Ate, si Tatay, si Nanay kasi nag-a-announce muna sila bago nila gawin. So may pagkakataon tayo na masawatan 'yung nangyayari,”…

blocks.text: Published October 8, 2026 3:41pm
Authorities have successfully prevented incidents of school violence from taking place, Justice Secretary Fredderick Vida said Thursday.

According to Vida, such incidents can be prevented, as there is a pattern in previous incidents where perpetrators would announce their intention beforehand. He cited the three school shooting incidents in Tacloban City, Zamboanga City, and Banga.

“Nag-a-announce muna, eh. Kaya sinabi ko maging mapagmatyag. Si Kuya, si Ate, si Tatay, si Nanay kasi nag-a-announce muna sila bago nila gawin. So may pagkakataon tayo na masawatan ‘yung nangyayari,” he said in a press briefing.

(They announce first. That’s why I said to be vigilant. Older brother, older sister, father, mother, because they announce first before they do it. So we have an opportunity to stop what is happening.)

“At naging successful na tayo. I just cannot give you details. I’ve been receiving reports. I saw reports. I read reports. Marami tayong successful na operations preventing ‘yung potential na incident,” he added.

(And we have already been successful. I just cannot give you details. I’ve been receiving reports. I saw reports. I read reports. We have had many successful operations preventing potential incidents.)
When asked how many incidents were prevented, Vida said the department will consolidate the reports.
Vida also said that authorities continue to monitor “groomers,” but the DOJ declined to give details as this is an ongoing operation.
Justice Undersecretary Michelle Ann Lapuz said that the Batang Ligtas Act was recently approved by the Senate and House of Representatives.

She said the bill expanded the coverage regarding the protection of children to include online recruitment, grooming, inducement of children to commit violent acts, as well as abuses involving artificial intelligence.
Lapuz stressed the importance of a whole-of-nation approach.
“Lahat may kanya-kanyang role dito. At ang batang ligtas, dine-define ‘yung roles ng bawat sector and the accountabilities kapag hindi na perform ‘yung mga responsibilities,” she said.
(Everyone has their own role here. And a child’s safety defines the roles of each sector and the accountabilities when the responsibilities are not performed.)
Lapuz expressed hope that the law will be passed before the National Children’s Month in November.
For his part, Vida called on parents to exercise their parental authority and to do their parental responsibility over their children.
He said that online platforms have tools that will allow parents to be informed about their children.

“Unfortunately, ang laging attitude lang ng magulang, ay hindi ko alam ‘yan. Bahala na siya. So itong mga bagay na ito, kapag hindi i-a-avail o hindi i-exercise ng magulang ang kanyang parental authority, hindi lang ito authority, and responsibility,” he said.

(Unfortunately, the usual attitude of parents is, “I don’t know about that. Let him be.” So these things, when the parent does not avail of or exercise their parental authority, it is not just authority; it is also a responsibility.)

“It’s not just about the authority. It’s about the responsibility. Hindi lang dahil naipanganak na ‘yan okay na ‘yan. Hindi dahil binabayaran mo ‘yung tuition, okay na ‘yan. Kailangan tayong magbantay. Kailangan natin bantayan at kalingain sila at gampanan natin kung ano ‘yung responsibillidad,” he added.

(It’s not just about the authority. It’s about the responsibility. Just because they have been born, that’s not enough. Just because you pay their tuition, that’s not enough. We need to watch over them. We need to watch over and care for them and fulfill our responsibilities.) —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Most UK diplomats to leave East Jerusalem consulate, Israel says, as Miliband says 'vital services' to remain
articles.summary: Israel said in September it would act in response to UK sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank.

blocks.text: Most diplomats will leave the British consulate in occupied East Jerusalem, Israel says, but the UK insists the building "will not be closing", and will operate as a "UK Mission"

"We did not want it to come to this," Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar wrote on social media, as he said 20 diplomats and the Consul General would leave Israel while a task force of seven could remain in the building "with a very limited scope of activity".
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband responded that some staff had been "temporarily withdrawn" for security reasons, but stressed the mission will "work with the Palestinian people".
Israel said in September it would shut the consulate, in retaliation for UK sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank which are illegal under international law.

The UK government had made last-ditch efforts to persuade Israel not to close the British consulate ahead of Thursday's deadline, after the Israeli government said it would close the consulate within 30 days of the UK sanctions announcement.
The consulate, which was first established in 1838, handles UK relations with Palestinians in Jerusalem as well as in the West Bank and Gaza.
It is distinct from the UK embassy in Tel Aviv, which is the UK's main diplomatic hub with Israel.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said the country had implemented measures announced on 8 September in response to UK sanctions.
"The British Consulate in Jerusalem is closing its operations today. Accordingly, the sign of the British Consulate in Jerusalem has been removed," he wrote on social media.
However, the British flag could still be seen outside and several staff were seen entering on Thursday morning.

Saar said talks with the UK government had resulted in agreement on certain principles, including that "the consul general and 20 diplomats (including the consul general) are ending their duties and will leave Israel."

But Saar acknowledged that the building is "the property of the British government" and said Israel had authorised "a task force of only seven diplomats with a very limited scope of activity" to operate in the building.
As a result of this agreement with the UK, he said, "no steps will be taken against Israel".
Israeli media had been reporting that the UK had threatened to expel Israeli diplomats from London - raising the prospect of further damaging bilateral relations.
In a written statement on the morning of the deadline, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the UK does not accept Israel has the right to close the consulate.
"The UK government reiterates its long-standing view that East Jerusalem is occupied territory."
Following discussions with the Israeli government, he said, the building "will not be closing" and will be known as the UK Mission, Jerusalem from Thursday.
However Miliband said an understanding had not been reached on "necessary assurances for the security and protections of our staff and premises".
"Accordingly the UK has temporarily withdrawn a number of staff and families to ensure their safety and security," he added.

articles.title: Sara Duterte camp files affidavit on Gracioso's cash delivery claims
articles.summary: The camp of Vice President Sara Duterte on Thursday submitted her affidavit to the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) regarding dismissed policeman Rodulfo Gracioso Jr.'s allegations that he…

blocks.text: Published October 8, 2026 3:02pm

The camp of Vice President Sara Duterte on Thursday submitted her affidavit to the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) regarding dismissed policeman Rodulfo Gracioso Jr.'s allegations that he delivered to her suitcases containing millions of pesos in cash.

"Nag-appear na po kami dito by way of special appearance tapos binigyan lang po namin sila ng kopya nung sinumpaang salaysalay, 'yung sinabi po ng ating bise presidente," lawyer Clifford Chua said in an ambush interview.
(We have already appeared here by way of special appearance, and we just gave them a copy of the sworn affidavit of what our Vice President said.)
Asked why Duterte was not present, Chua said that she is not required to appear before the bureau.
To recall, Gracioso claimed to deliver cash to the vice president, Davao Representative Paolo Duterte, and former president Rodrigo Duterte on the instructions of former speaker Lord Allan Velasco.
Duterte read out her affidavit in a press briefing on Tuesday, denying his claims.
Chua said they also submitted the photos presented by the vice president during her press briefing.
The vice president has said Gracioso was motivated by money and resentment towards Velasco and his family.

Velasco's camp on Saturday called out "fabricated attacks" against him, saying these have "no basis." It also called out accusations against Velasco as "inconsistent," tailored as a "one-size fits all" narration.
In an interview on Balitanghali, NBI Director Melvin Matibag said the the bureau will review Duterte's affidavit.

articles.title: British consulate in East Jerusalem will stay open as UK mission, says Ed Miliband
articles.summary:
Foreign secretary says former consulate general will remain independent, operational ⁠and serving Palestinian people

The foreign secretary, ⁠Ed Miliband, has said Britain’s consulate general…

blocks.text: The foreign secretary, ⁠Ed Miliband, has said Britain’s consulate general ⁠building in ⁠East Jerusalem ​will not be closing but will ⁠be known as a UK mission, remaining independent, operational ⁠and serving Palestinian people.
Israel had ​ordered the ‌British consulate ‌in East Jerusalem to close ‌on Thursday over the UK’s plans to impose sanctions on settlements in the West Bank.
Miliband said that having ‌withdrawn a number of staff and families in recent ​weeks, it would now work to build up its presence.
He said Britain would ⁠not take any reciprocal action ​against Israel ​while the ​two sides engaged in ​talks, ‌following speculation it ​could expel some Israeli diplomats from Britain.

Diplomats from other western countries had been worried about any closure setting a precedent, and suggested Britain had to respond strongly to the Israeli move because it had implications beyond the immediate dispute.

The consulate is separate from the UK embassy, based in Tel Aviv, and has a distinct diplomatic role, covering East Jerusalem, the rest of the West Bank and Gaza, where it provides consular services to Palestinians.

Israel had threatened to close it in protest at the UK’s decision to ban trade in goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, said Britain’s ‌decision to impose sanctions was “morally distorted” and accused the governing Labour party of being hostile towards his country.

The ‌incident has highlighted growing frustration among Israel’s longtime allies over its settlements in the occupied West Bank, viewed by much of the world as illegal under international law. In his statement to the UK parliament, Miliband said settler terrorists, supported by Netanyahu’s government, were committing ethnic cleansing in the West Bank. Israel disputes this.

The UK Foreign Office was advised informally by the former attorney general Dominic Grieve that Israel would be acting unlawfully if it closed the consulate on the basis it was sited in East Jerusalem, which is recognised by the United Nations and most of its members, including the UK, as being occupied Palestinian territory.
after newsletter promotion

Israel has also said it will revoke the credentials of Dutch diplomats from the country’s mission to Palestine in response to the Netherlands’ ban on imports from illegal Israeli settlements. France and Canada, which joined the UK in the settlement trade ban, have not had action taken against them.

UK-Israeli relations have deteriorated steadily during the war in Gaza, prompted by Hamas’s 7 October 2023 massacre of Israelis, as Britain became increasingly critical of the way in which Netanyahu seemed prepared to tolerate the deaths of thousands of Palestinians in an effort to render Hamas inoperative, a task successive Westminster governments thought was unachievable through his methods.

The UK has rescinded a large number of arms export licences to Israel and Miliband has spoken of evidence of war crimes in Gaza. He has declined to accuse Israel of genocide on the grounds he believes this is a matter for international courts to determine.

blocks.text: US prosecutors are expected to bring new charges against ousted Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores over the alleged torture of Americans held in Venezuela, a US official said late on Wednesday.
The charges could be announced as soon as Thursday and reportedly concern the alleged wrongful detention of more than a dozen US citizens during Maduro's 13-year rule.
Prosecutors are also considering charges against others allegedly involved in the torture.
Details of the potential new charges and the alleged victims were not immediately available.
Maduro's wife seeks release
Meanwhile, the 69-year-old Flores is due in Manhattan federal court on Thursday where she is expected to ask a judge to release her from jail and place her under house arrest, citing health problems.
Her lawyers say she has lost 25 pounds in custody, suffers from dizziness and shortness of breath and may have suffered a minor heart attack in July.
They have proposed that she live at a New York residence under 24-hour security.

blocks.caption: Media reports said prosecutors are also considering charging several other people for their alleged role in torturing Americans [FILE: March 26, 2026]Image: Jane Rosenberg/REUTERS

blocks.text: Prosecutors, however, oppose the request, arguing that Flores poses an "extreme risk of flight and danger to the public” if released.
They said she has received hospital treatment when necessary, while in custody.
Trump vs Maduro
Maduro, 63, and Flores are being held at a federal detention center in Brooklyn as they await their trial in June next year.
The couple was captured during an unprecedented middle-of-the-night raid on their Caracas home on January 3, which was hailed by US President Donald Trump as a "surgical law enforcement operation."
Critics have accused Trump of operating outside international law.
They were subsequently brought to New York, where they face existing drug trafficking and firearms charges.
Maduro has maintained his innocence, calling himself a prisoner of war and referring to his capture as a kidnapping.

Meanwhile, in August, Trump announced that the US had reached a deal to take control of part of Venezuela's vast oil reserves, which Venezuelan Interim President Delcy Rodriguez also termed "historic."

articles.title: Supreme Court eases process for recognizing foreign divorces in Philippines
articles.summary: In the high court’s En Banc session on October 7, the Court said the new rules eliminate the requirement that petitioners independently prove the foreign divorce law in court, requiring them…

blocks.text: This file photo shows the seal of the Supreme Court.
Philstar.com / EC Toledo

MANILA, Philippines — The Supreme Court has approved amendments to the Rules of Court that streamline the legal process for Filipino spouses seeking Philippine judicial recognition of foreign divorces.

In the high court’s En Banc session on October 7, the Court said the new rules eliminate the requirement that petitioners independently prove the foreign divorce law in court, requiring them only to establish that the divorce decree was issued.

The newly introduced provision under Rule 39 establishes a legal presumption that a foreign divorce obtained between a Filipino and a foreign spouse is absolute and allows the foreign spouse to remarry under foreign law, unless the decree explicitly specifies that it is a limited divorce.
Under the amended rules, the burden of proof shifts to the opposing party to show that a foreign divorce is not absolute.

Furthermore, English translations of divorce documents are presumed accurate if certified under oath by the translator — a presumption that may be contested with contrary evidence, such as certified true copies of foreign divorce laws sourced from the Office of the Court Administrator's central repository.
“These presumptions are disputable, meaning they may be challenged with contrary evidence, under Section 3 of Rule 131,” the Supreme Court’s statement read.

“To challenge these presumptions, Section 24 of Rule 132 allows the submission of a certified true copy of the applicable foreign divorce law, including its English translation, obtained from the Office of the Court Administrator (OCA), which will maintain a repository of foreign laws,” it added.
However, the Supreme Court clarified that the core legal framework under Article 26(2) of the Family Code remains unchanged.
Filipino spouses must still file a formal petition for judicial recognition in Philippine courts.
Furthermore, petitions may still be opposed on established legal grounds, including lack of jurisdiction, lack of notice, fraud, or clear mistakes of law or fact.
Addressing challenges of OFWs

According to the High Court, it introduced these procedural changes after recognizing the significant hurdles Filipino spouses — especially Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs) — face in proving foreign statutes.

Citing Department of Foreign Affairs findings, the high court noted that obtaining official certifications and English translations across varied international jurisdictions created unnecessary barriers, which these amendments seek to eliminate.

blocks.text: Senator-judge Mark Villar attends Day 2 of the impeachment trial at the Senate in Pasay City.
Mark Villar via Facebook
MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Mark Villar has regained chairship of the powerful Senate public works committee in his jump to the majority bloc.

Majority Leader Sen. Juan Miguel Zubiri confirmed Villar's switch to the majority during the plenary session Thursday, October 8, where he also announced Villar's election as chair of the public works panel, replacing Sen. Tito Sotto.
The Senate has also elected Villar as a member of the Commission on Appointments, replacing Zubiri.
The majority bloc now has 14 members.
Alongside the reshuffle, Minority Leader Sen. Alan Peter Cayetano was also elected as member of the Commission on Appointments, replacing Sen. Loren Legarda.
Mark's sister, Sen. Camille Villar, remains in the Cayetano-led minority bloc.
Mark previously broke with the minority bloc during the impeachment court's deliberations on whether to do away with the fixed 16-vote threshold for convicting Vice President Sara Duterte.
The senator had voted in favor of allowing the court to interpret with flexibility the Constitution's requirement of conviction by "two-thirds of all members" of the Senate.
Ombudsman probe
Both Villar siblings are facing an Ombudsman probe for alleged violations of the anti-graft law over joint ventures entered into by their former water utility firm PrimeWater Infrastructure Corp.

Besides the two sitting senators, the Ombudsman also named former Senators Manny and Cynthia Villar, businessman Manuel Paolo Villar, as well as PrimeWater executives Fe Reblancos and Romeo Sabater as respondents in the criminal and administrative complaints.
PrimeWater has been accused of entering into deals with local water districts between 2015 and 2022 that were skewed against the government's interest.
The agreements under scrutiny were signed during Mark's term as public works secretary and membership on the board of the Local Water Utilities Administration.

articles.title: Bachelor star Sam Wood denied bail as police allege he choked woman until she ‘thought she would die’
articles.summary:
Court hears police attended Wood’s Victorian home over a similar allegation about three years ago, but the woman had not complained then out of ‘fear of retribution’

  • Get our

blocks.text: A woman who was allegedly choked and assaulted by the former Bachelor star Sam Wood told police she “thought she was going to die”, a Queensland court heard on Thursday.

The court also heard that police in Victoria had attended Wood’s home in relation to a similar incident about three years ago, but that the woman had not wanted to make a complaint at that time out of “fear of retribution”.

Wood, a 46-year-old wellness influencer from Melbourne, was denied bail in a Queensland court on Thursday and will be held in custody indefinitely awaiting trial, after police argued his behaviour was “escalating” and that he posed an unacceptable risk.

Wood appeared in court via video link from the Maroochydore police watch house cells, where he had been held for about four days. He was arrested at Noosa on the Sunshine Coast on Sunday and charged with two domestic violence offences: assault occasioning bodily harm and strangulation in a domestic setting.

In outlining the prosecution case, police prosecutor Jeanette Grigoris said the brief of evidence included a triple zero call made by a family member, photographs of the victim’s injuries, and a video-recorded statement by the complainant.
Grigoris said the complainant was supportive of the charges proceeding.
Wood’s lawyer has indicated the reality TV star will fight the charges.
The court heard that in the video statement, the woman alleges she was choked and that “there was a cessation of breath”.
“She articulates the banging of her head on the floor. She couldn’t breathe,” Grigoris said.
“She thought she was going to die.”
Grigoris said the video statement by the woman also refers to a previous matter in Victoria “being of a similar nature” and “involved choking”.
The court heard that in a police interview, recorded about midnight on Sunday morning.
Wood denied that any previous incident had taken place in Victoria.
Grigoris said there was body-worn camera footage of police attending his home and a police report in relation to that incident.
Grigoris said the woman “did not make any criminal complaints on that occasion, she was in fear of retribution of the defendant.”
Grigoris also raised concern that Wood, during his police interview, minimised his part in the alleged offending, and minimised the injuries suffered by the woman.
“He’s essentially victim blamed,” she said.
Wood’s lawyer, Matthew Cuskelly, sought bail and said his client denied the allegations. He cited a psychologist’s report that said Wood was suffering from “severe depression”.
“He ought to be given the opportunity to engage with mental health professionals,” Cuskelly said.
“And also try to salvage something of his professional reputation and career, which is taking a hell of a beating at the moment.

“Ultimately, as all families have, there was problems. And my client had been enduring the hardship of attempting to quarantine those problems from his family for some period of time. It was agonising.”
Cuskelly cited a psychologist’s report that describes ‘the difficulty that my client has been enduring in respect of the deterioration of his psychological state”.
“His depression is regarded as extremely severe.”
Cuskelly said Wood had no prior criminal history and if granted bail would reside in Victoria with his father, Andrew Wood, who attended the court in support of his son.
Acting magistrate Janelle Boegheim said she was not satisfied by the defence argument that the case against Wood was weak.
“The strength of the evidence against the defendant is … relatively strong at this juncture.”
Boegheim said it was likely the charges, if proven, would attract a term in prison.
Wood was stood down by his own fitness empire, 28 by Sam Wood, on Monday, a day after he was charged.
“We have all been shocked and saddened by the matters involving Sam Wood,” said Mark Watkin, the group’s acting chief executive.
“We have zero tolerance for domestic violence. While the matter is under investigation and before the court, Sam is on indefinite leave from his duties.
“Our thoughts are with the family and anyone in the community affected by domestic violence.”
He is due to face court again on November 23.

articles.title: Thursday briefing: Why young people are taking to the streets across France
articles.summary:
In today’s newsletter: A youth-led movement is protesting crumbling school buildings and teacher shortages while turning adult focus onto wider educational inequalities

Good morning.…

blocks.text: Good morning. In my experience, at any protest, the most memorable and encapsulating slogans are always the ones written by hand with marker pen on cardboard placards.

“School is a right, not a privilege,” read one such sign held aloft by a student in Paris, where huge youth protests over the state of high school education have brought tens of thousands of young people and adults on to the streets, with further strikes planned today.
“A state that gasses high school students is a weak state,” another sign said, referencing growing public anger at alleged police brutality towards young protesters.

Tens of thousands of young people have also taken to Spanish streets in recent weeks to protest against the country’s deepening housing crisis. And outside the Labour conference in Liverpool last week, a crowd of jobless young people protested against what they saw as their bleak employment prospects. From Paris to the north of England, a similar thread runs through it all: a generation who feel betrayed by the absence of basic economic security and the erosion of public services that older generations took for granted.
I spoke to our Paris correspondent Angelique Chrisafis who has been reporting from the centre of the French protests. But first, the headlines.
Five big stories

items: UK politics | Kemi Badenoch has announced that the Conservatives would abolish inheritance tax on family homes if elected, prompting criticism that she is prioritising cutting taxes for the rich.

Education | Labour’s flagship changes to special education in England are at risk of unravelling because parents are rushing to secure support for their children before the system changes, new analysis has found.
Spain | María del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old whose eviction set off a nationwide wave of protests against Spain’s housing crisis, has died.
Science | A type of gene therapy based on Nobel prize-winning science is safe and can partly restore sight in blind people, researchers have revealed.
Epstein | British billionaire Sir James Goldsmith warned that Jeffrey Epstein was a “sexual deviant” decades before the FBI closed in on the abuser, a Guardian investigation has found.

blocks.text: In depth: Why have young people taken to the streets?

blocks.caption: ‘School is a right, not a privilege’ … students take to the streets in Paris. Photograph: Sarah Meyssonnier/Reuters

blocks.text: The most significant youth movement to emerge across France in recent decades started on 17 September. Pupils returning to the Lycée Saint-Exupéry in Créteil, southwest of Paris, after the summer holidays, discovered they couldn’t continue their studies because of the extent of staff absences. The 15- to 18-year-olds blockaded their high school in protest.

After negotiations with the education ministry, those staffing gaps were filled, but the impassioned complaints about crumbling buildings, overcrowded classrooms, and long school days – alongside a wider sense of inequality in the education system – resonated in the suburbs. “This movement grew from the ground up, from teenagers speaking to others outside their lycées. And over a couple of weeks, it has spread to hundreds of schools across France,” Angelique tells me.

There’s a tendency to mythologise youth protest, especially in France – my uncle Joss was in Paris in 1968, and I lapped up his tales of pulling up cobblestones with his bare hands to build barricades. But youth activism is often diminished. When I reported on the schoolchildren who protested against the war in Iraq in 2003, and those who took part in climate strikes more than a decade later, adults repeatedly questioned whether they were swayed by older provocateurs or just wanted an excuse to dodge school and indulge in petty vandalism. (In my experience: no, no and no.)

So it is in France this past month. “This is very much a youth movement,” says Angelique, comparing it to similar protests in 2006 over an unpopular youth employment contract, which were organised by students’ unions. “High schoolers are organising themselves without a centralised system or even spokesperson. That’s historic, and it’s taken the government by surprise.”
Who are the teenagers on the streets?

This week, the sociologist Fabien Truong, who has written widely on youth protest culture, praised the “maturity and coherence” of the protesters. He pointed to a “social media effect” whereby teenagers in wealthier areas were sharing videos of scurrying rats, gaping ceilings and leaking toilets in poorer schools. “It’s beautiful, this solidarity with students from more privileged backgrounds fighting for others and more equality.”

This is precisely what Angelique has witnessed on the streets of Paris in recent days, where some of the most elite state schools have also been barricaded. She spoke to one teacher outside a school in a richer inner-city area, who was proud of her pupils. “She said there was a feeling of solidarity and generosity between teenagers, and how it flies in the face of the idea that they’re part of a social media generation who are selfish and narcissistic.”

“I spent a long time speaking to teenage girls at one of the barricades in the centre of the city,” Angelique says,“who were sitting on top of a pile of bins and shopping trolleys. They told me: ‘We’re told in France that state education is a great leveller, but that’s not the case. We are being taught our lessons, but we’re getting out on to the street because we can’t bear to know that other students in poorer areas are in buildings that are crumbling’.”

***What’s wrong with French schools?As Angelique sets out in this helpful explainer, the pupils’ grievances are backed up by evidence – and the prime minister himself has described them as “legitimate”. Thousands of French schools at all levels, both primary and secondary, are in need of repair. Class sizes are bigger on average, and school days are longer, than in other comparable countries, while about 10% of teaching hours across the year are not delivered because of absent teachers.

And yet France’s expenditure on high schools is 28% higher than the OECD average. What’s going on? The high spend can be explained in various ways, Angelique tells me. France has a lot more high school buildings to maintain than other countries, and many more vocational courses that cost more to teach.

At the same time, more spending is desperately needed on staff. Teacher shortages are linked to very low pay progression through the profession, while there are severe difficulties in finding teachers to work in deprived areas. There’s also a shortfall in other crucial roles, including school nurses and support staff for pupils with disabilities.
How have adults responded?

Angelique tells me that what has defined how adults are responding to this burgeoning movement is the behaviour of politicians and police. Initially, the French government “had its head in the sand”, she says, distracted by public anger at rising fuel costs and a difficult budget process. “And when it suddenly woke up, the reaction was not a political one, it was a police crackdown.”

Eighteen investigations into possible police brutality are already under way after injuries allegedly involving the use of police weapons, including a 15-year-old who lost his hand after contact with a stun grenade and a 14-year-old whose jaw was shattered after police allegedly beat him and fired a form of rubber-bullet launcher.

Yesterday, the French interior minister suspended the use of stun grenades but rejected accusations of police brutality, saying riot officers only intervened when protesters turned violent. Dozens of teachers have also been injured in clashes, and a small number of schools burned or ransacked, but Angelique tells me that most protests have been peaceful.

The injuries, however, have prompted outrage, with parents and teachers angry at the “disproportionate police response” now joining young people at the barricades. An Elabe poll for BFMTV, published on Wednesday, found that 72% of French people thought the student’s demands were legitimate – although 55% of of those surveyed also thought the protests should come to an end.

The movement has also brought to the fore a debate about the wider state of public services ahead of next year’s presidential election. The radical left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, backed for president by 47% of voters under 35, is loudly supporting the protesters, while far-right candidate Marine Le Pen has blamed the current government for chaos and called for an anti-riot law.

The sheer scale of the marches in cities across France this week was unexpected, Angelique says. “There were hundreds of thousands of parents, grandparents and teachers. There is a lot of support for these young people’s demands and an understanding that the problems they are raising reflect wider worries about public services.”

blocks.text: At 65 years old, Luis Gómez was still hawking vegetables at the market he had worked at since the age of eight. Now at 80, Gomes, or JM as he is popularly known, has become a musical sensation, selling out venues across Chile, as well as in Mexico, the UK, Argentina and France. He is the frontman of Los Crack del Puerto, who in May released their fourth record, Lo Mucho Que Nos Queda (So Much Yet to Come), as a cassette – to great acclaim.

It’s a long way from his early life in the city of Valparaíso; the youngest of five children, he was three when his father died, and 10 when he lost his mother. For a time, he slept on the street between parked cars. JM would eventually form a musical double act with his cousin, Juan Navarro, and the two entertained crowds in Valparaíso’s bars. The pair would find fame well into their 70s after forming the band in 2017. “I never planned any of this, and I’d be happy still working at the market,” JM says. “But I suppose it’s never too late to give something a try.”

articles.title: PhilHealth underfunding limits improved benefits — solon
articles.summary: According to Montes, the proposed P74.4 billion PhilHealth budget for 2027 falls short from the P75.2 projected collections from sin taxes for tobacco and sweetened beverages alone.

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Persistent underfunding has prevented the Philippine Health Insurance Corp. from improving its health benefit packages for its members, a lawmaker said on Thursday, October 8.

House Minority Leader Iris Marie Montes claimed on Thursday, October 8, that the country’s national health insurer has remained underfunded for years even after the passage of the Universal Health Care Act in 2019.

“Sa mga nakaraang taon po, simula po kasi noong naisabatas natin ang Universal Health Care Law, ay mano-notice po natin na hindi po naibibigay nang tama ‘yung pondong dapat sa PhilHealth,” Monte said in an interview with dzMM.
(In the past years, ever since we passed the Universal Health Care Law into law, we have noticed that the appropriate funds for PhilHealth are not properly given.)

The lawmaker also claimed that the mandated earmarks under the law, or the designated funds from sin taxes and shares from the Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corp. (PAGCOR) and the Philippine Charity Sweepstakes Office (PCSO) for PhilHealth, were not fully and accurately allocated to the agency.
According to Montes, the proposed P74.4 billion PhilHealth budget for 2027 falls short of the P75.2 projected collections from sin taxes for tobacco and sweetened beverages alone.
“Ang nilagay lang po nila tobacco and sweetened beverages; hindi pa nga po kasama ‘yung alcohol and vapor products,” Montes said. “Kulang na nga po ano."
(They only included tobacco and sweetened beverages, not alcohol and vapor products.)
Automatic appropriation
Montes argued that a Supreme Court ruling last year and several measures constitute that under the Universal Healthcare Act, the mandated earmarks must be automatically appropriated to PhilHealth.

The lawmaker was referring to the SC ruling on consolidated petitions on the PhilHealth case in December 2025, ordering the return of a P60-billion excess fund that the Department of Finance (DOF) had ordered to be transferred to the National Treasury.

“With the ruling of the Supreme Court, dapat po malinaw na ito sa DBM (Department of Budget and Management) at sa Kongreso na itong mga earmarks dito ay dapat awtomatikong mapunta sa PhilHealth,” Montes said.
(With the Supreme Court’s ruling, it should be clear to DBM and to Congress that these earmarks must be automatically allotted to PhilHealth.)
Limited benefits
Section 11 of the Universal Health Care Act provides that the PhilHealth must maintain reserve funds with a ceiling of equivalent to two years of projected program expenses.
PhilHealth is required to utilize the excess from these reserve funds to improve the National Health Insurance Program (NHIP) and reduce member contributions.
With the persistent underfunding of PhilHealth, Montes said the public health insurer struggles to provide better health packages and plan for any improvements due to limited financial certainty.

Additionally, the lack of budget predictability, which according to Montes, helps to achieve universal health care, prevents PhilHealth from strategically planning and instead pushes it to reactive spending.

articles.title: NSW police commissioner made last-minute bid to hold closed-door hearings into Sydney anti-Herzog protest
articles.summary:
Police watchdog says Mal Lanyon’s timing in raising the issue was ‘regrettable’ and led to delays

  • Get our

blocks.text: The New South Wales police commissioner made a last-minute bid to hold hearings into Sydney’s anti-Herzog protest behind closed doors, delaying the inquiry, the police watchdog has revealed.

The Law Enforcement Conduct Commission (Lecc) has said that its inquiry into the February protest at Sydney’s town hall, launched after widespread allegations of police brutality, would go ahead this month with a mix of public and private examinations, saying the timing of issues raised by police commissioner, Mal Lanyon, was “regrettable”.

Lecc launched an investigation after the protest on 9 February, during which numerous protesters – and 10 officers – were injured, including demonstrators in their 70s and 80s. Viral video footage showed police punching multiple protesters, and grabbing Muslim worshippers while they undertook their sunset prayers.
Thirty people were charged in the months after the protest, but four have since had their charges dropped. More than 20 of those charged are due to face a joint hearing next July.

In a decision made public on Thursday, the Lecc chief commissioner, Peter Johnson SC, revealed that legal representatives for Lanyon had indicated for the “first time” on 9 September that he wished to be heard on the issue of public and private examinations. The bid was made less than two weeks before the public hearings between September and November were due to start. Some hearings were also expected to be heard in private.

“The timing of these issues being raised by the Commissioner of Police is more than regrettable given its impact on the orderly progress of the investigation, the preparation for examinations and the efficient and effective use of public resources by both the Commission and the NSWPF and the associated cost and disruption flowing from the delay,” Johnson said.
Johnson said the start date of public hearings, 21 September, was subsequently delayed to “a date to be fixed” to allow a private hearing for submissions on the issue.

Lawyers acting on behalf of Lanyon submitted that Lecc’s opening address and the examination of witnesses should occur in private and not be livestreamed. They argued that the Lecc Act does not have the power to hear “broad ranging open submissions” and said Lecc should not take the “unconventional approach of hearing opening submissions in public part way through an investigation that is already underway”.

But Lecc argued that it does have the power to decide when public examinations are appropriate. The counsel assisting submitted that public examinations were necessary because “there was already significant information concerning the events of 9 February 2026 in the public domain, including footage of use of force by police” and that senior police officers had advanced in public an “official narrative of what took place”.
“Public comments made by senior police increase the need for independent scrutiny,” the commissioner wrote.

The counsel assisting had pointed to specific features of the investigation as reason for why only private examinations were not appropriate. This included the “significant public concern” after the protest, including in parts of the Islamic community in Western Sydney.

On Thursday, the watchdog said its inquiry into the protest would begin with a public address by counsel assisting on 19 October, followed by five weeks of private hearings. Lecc expects senior officers will then appear at public examinations.

It said its Operation Makalu inquiry would analyse the use of OC spray, as well as the “improper use of arrest powers and the police use of force” at the protest. It will consider police planning ahead of the protest and “any opportunities for improvement in the policing of protests”.
after newsletter promotion

In his decision, the commissioner determined that private examinations would be held on “issues of fact” while public examinations would be held to deal with systemic issues, but only after the private examinations have been held.

In September, Palestinian Australian Eyad Shadid launched a civil case in the NSW district court, alleging he was assaulted, battered and falsely imprisoned by police near Sydney’s town hall. He alleged in his statement of claim that NSW police committed misfeasance in public office and subjected him to a malicious prosecution.

In a statement, NSW Greens justice spokesperson, Sue Higginson, described the push to hold hearings in private as “an extraordinary attempt by the police to suppress the public examination of allegations of serious misconduct by uniformed police officers, and to prevent public scrutiny of the political decisions and command structures that led to police violence against protesters”.

At a NSW parliamentary inquiry in May, Johnson said police had become “overly defensive” in response to requests for information in its investigations, describing the relationship between the agencies as “difficult”. He said the Lecc had received a record number of complaints, more than 800, as part of its investigation into the Herzog protest.
In a statement following Johnson’s comments, NSW police said it “complied with the requirements of the LECC Act in a cooperative manner”.
NSW police said in a statement it acknowledged the decision to hold private hearings and awaited the findings.

image.caption: The Houthis have repeatedly sought to disrupt Saudi air travel [File: September 19, 2026]Image: REUTERS

blocks.text: Yemen's Houthi rebels say they struck Saudi Arabia's main international airport in the capital, Riyadh, with a missile attack on Thursday.
They said the strike killed three people and injured several others. It was the third time this weekthat the armed group claimed to have targeted the airport.

"Our armed forces successfully targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with a ballistic missile, which accurately struck its target and disrupted airport operations," Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said on X.
The conflict in Yemen has increasingly spilled across the country's borders since reigniting in July.

A day earlier, the Saudi-backed and internationally recognized Yemeni government announced a major counteroffensive against the Houthis, who are fighting government forces for control of additional territory.
At the same time, the rebels also warned passenger airlines to stop flying through Saudi airspace.
"We reiterate our call and warning, for the last time, to all international airlines against continuing to operate flights through Saudi airspace," Saree said.
Can Yemen's government turn the tide against the Houthis?
What is the status of the conflict?
According to the United Nations (UN), the conflict has displaced more than 200,000 people within Yemen.
This week, the Yemeni government claimed to have pushed Houthi fighters out of strategic areas along the Red Sea coast and around the port city of Mocha.

Coalition forces spokesperson Turki al-Maliki said that 82 Houthi military targets had been destroyed in the Yemeni provinces of Saada, Marib, Al Jawf, and Al Hudaydah. Al-Maliki did not provide details about casualties or damage, and his claims could not be independently verified.
The targets reportedly included missile launch sites, command centers, and missile and weapons depots.

articles.title: Margaret Hamilton, whose software helped land Apollo 11 on the Moon, dies at 90
articles.summary: Pioneering computer scientist led the development of the software for Nasa's Apollo mission and was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom.

blocks.text: The computer scientist behind groundbreaking research that helped land Nasa's astronauts on the Moon, has died aged 90.
Margaret Hamilton was a trailblazer in her field, leading the team who developed the software for Nasa's Apollo missions, which coined the term "software engineering".
Hamilton's former employer, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), confirmed her death, adding she died on 30 September.

"To say Hamilton was a pioneer - to say she was ahead of her time - would be a dramatic understatement," MIT said in its statement, before acknowledging that she was a software engineer before it was mainstream.
Hamilton worked at MIT from 1959 until the mid-1970s and managed the Software Engineering Division.

It was in this division that she led a team of engineers writing and testing all onboard in-flight software for Nasa's Apollo 11 project that guided US astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin to land safely on the Moon.
"I was attracted both by the sheer idea and the fact that it had never been done before. I was the first programmer to join and the first woman they hired," she told the Guardian in 2019.
In 1969, moments before the historic Apollo 11 Moon landing, an onboard computer raised an alarm, signalling an error was occurring.
The error detected the computer was overloaded, and for a moment it looked like the complex landing might not be achieved.

But Hamilton and her team had planned for such an error by engineering "priority-driven software" to shut down any background tasks and favour the most important - the Moon landing - according to MIT.
The team's famous software engineering was immortalised in a 1969 photograph of Hamilton standing beside the stack of printed code that towered beside her.
In 2016, Hamilton's life work was honoured by Barack Obama with the Presidential Medal of Freedom for her contribution to science and space travel.
At the time, Obama said Hamilton "symbolises that generation of unsung women who helped send humankind into space".
Hamilton, born in Indiana in 1936, first studied mathematics at the University of Michigan in 1955 before moving to Earlham College where she got a BA in mathematics in 1958.
She then moved to Boston, Massachusetts, a year later with her husband and originally took the job at MIT to support her husband during his law degree.
From the 1970s onwards, Hamilton used her expertise to found her own software businesses, including Hamilton Technologies, which is still based in Massachusetts.
"We are saddened by her death, but grateful for the opportunity to have celebrated her extraordinary achievements throughout her long life", Earlham College said in a statement on social media.
"Her pioneering spirit and remarkable legacy will continue to inspire generations of Earlhamites," the statement said.
Hamilton is survived by her daughter, a son-in-law, two grandsons and four great-grandchildren, according to MIT.

articles.title: US and Lebanon protecting wanted Syrian general, BBC finds
articles.summary: Bassam al-Hassan, linked to reporter Austin Tice's abduction, is being sheltered in return for information.

blocks.text: A former Syrian general wanted for crimes against humanity, external is being bankrolled and protected by the US and Lebanese authorities, a BBC News investigation has found.

Bassam al-Hassan, who oversaw Syria's chemical weapons programme and was a senior adviser to former President Bashar al-Assad, is being harboured in Lebanon following the Assad regime's collapse in 2024.

An investigation by the BBC and the US broadcaster NPR has discovered that Hassan has been allowed to remain there under an arrangement involving the FBI, and other US and Lebanese authorities. This is because of his willingness to provide information about the abduction of American journalist Austin Tice in Syria in 2012, as well as additional intelligence, we have been told.
Last month the BBC revealed Tice's abduction had been a planned operation, with Hassan in the chain of command.

Officials from two different branches of Syria's new government have told the BBC they want Hassan returned to face trial, but that US authorities want him kept in Lebanon, and they say there is little Damascus can do about this.

We asked the FBI, the CIA and Lebanon's General Directorate of General Security to comment on our findings. Only the FBI responded, declining to comment and instead directing us to a past statement that said its focus remained on establishing the facts around the Tice case and securing his return.

In response to our findings, Phil Elwood, spokesperson for the Tice family said: "If what you are saying is true, the fact that our tax dollars are being used to furnish a comfortable life for someone associated with the use of chemical weapons on Syrian civilians, who claims to have had Austin Tice executed, is offensive.
"This is nothing less than aiding and abetting the escape of a wanted war criminal. The Syrians deserve justice and he should be returned to stand trial."

As part of a years-long investigation featured in the new BBC podcast: Where is Austin Tice? Series 3 of I'm Not A Monster Presents, the BBC has reviewed a detailed record of a meeting between Hassan, FBI and CIA representatives, and Lebanese security officials, where Tice's case is discussed.
In it, Hassan is offered "residency", "protection" and help securing his "living needs" in return for information, primarily about Tice.

Sources with knowledge of the arrangement confirmed this was the case, and described to us how Hassan receives money from the US authorities through an intermediary, making it harder to trace. Hassan is sanctioned by the US government.

Yet people connected to the Tice investigation say they have seen little evidence it has significantly advanced since Hassan began providing information as part of this agreement. The deal is believed to have been struck in the spring of 2025.
Sources with knowledge of the investigation have expressed concerns that Hassan's arrangement with the US could continue indefinitely, at significant expense but with little gain.
Hassan is not the only Syrian regime official whose connection to the Tice case has seemingly afforded him financial payments or assistance for living abroad.

One former regime member said he had received money from the FBI multiple times in exchange for his co-operation on Tice's case. It was "not in his interest to share all the information all at once," he told the BBC, "in order to be able to drag out how long he can continue to receive payments from them [the US authorities]".
Another former regime member connected to the Tice case claimed he was living in Lebanon under the "patronage" of the US authorities, citing this as the reason he could not speak to us about Tice.

The BBC spoke to a former senior Lebanese intelligence official who confirmed that Lebanese intelligence does have arrangements with the Americans, and that these types of payments have and do take place when both agencies have overlap in cases, but said he had no knowledge of payments involving the Tice case.

Hassan told US investigators last year that Tice had been executed on former President Assad's orders, but several people with knowledge of the investigation have questioned the details of his account. Hassan has provided a potential location for Tice's remains, but when the site was searched, nothing was found - according to multiple sources familiar with the dig - casting doubt on the validity of some of Hassan's information.

There are questions, however, over how thoroughly the site was searched. Two sources who said they had intimate knowledge of the operation told the BBC that US authorities stopped digging before the search had been completed, possibly because of security concerns.
When the BBC managed to reach Hassan by phone last year to ask for an interview, he directed us to seek permission for him to speak from the FBI and CIA at the US embassy in Beirut.
Our investigation has found that other Syrian officials connected to the Tice case have also apparently found refuge abroad.

They include Mohammad Makhlouf, who reported to Hassan in Syria and was connected to Tice's detention - now believed to be residing in Lebanon. And Sakr Rustom, Hassan's nephew who was involved in Tice's abduction, now believed to be moving between the UAE and Lebanon. When the BBC attempted to speak to Rustom about Tice's case, he said he "preferred to focus on matters of the future".

Ghassan Nassour, a former general in Syria's Republican Guard, is said by former members of the National Defence Forces to have presided over the jail Tice was held in, and is believed to be living in the UAE with his family, we have been told.

articles.title: ‘That is a lie’: alleged Alan Jones victim denies family tried to get money out of broadcaster, court hears
articles.summary:
Youngest complainant in trial alleges Jones put his tongue in his mouth and touched him on the bottom during visit to shock jock’s property

  • Get our

blocks.text: An alleged teenage victim of Alan Jones has denied his family tried to deceive the broadcaster and get as much money out of him as they could during a tense cross-examination in a Sydney court.
Asked whether he was intent on getting as much financial assistance as he could from the former 2GB host, the witness replied: “That is a lie.”

The youngest complainant in the trial has told the court he was 17 when Jones allegedly put his tongue inside his mouth and touched him on the bottom during a visit to the shock jock’s property in the Southern Highlands.
Known as complainant A, the witness said he visited the Fitzroy Falls farm several years after he started corresponding with Jones at the age of 13.
He posted a letter to Jones asking for help after his father left, a family member died and his single mother was struggling financially.
Complainant A is one of five men who allege Jones indecently assaulted or sexually touched them between 2003 and 2020.
The host has pleaded not guilty to 21 charges of indecent assault and sexual touching.

Jones’s barrister, Gabrielle Bashir SC, has been cross-examining the young man for two days about the extent of his mother’s involvement in the hundreds of emails which were sent to Jones between 2013 and 2016.
The witness has accepted that his mother provided financial details and documents and made suggestions about what to write, but insisted the correspondence was largely his own work.
Bashir asked: “Were you trying to deceive Mr Jones about the author of the email when you sent emails just signed off from [A] that your mother had input into?”
Complainant A replied: “No.”
Bashir said: “I suggest that you were - what do you say to that?”
A replied: “That you’re wrong.”
Bashir took the witness to a particular email and asked the witness if he agreed that he wanted Jones’s assistance with his mother’s mortgage.
The complainant repeatedly refused to agree, saying “I am not going to be railroaded” and “I am not going to have my words twisted, Ms Bashir”.
Bashir asked: “You understood your mother had the intention of obtaining as much assistance from Mr Jones as she could?”
A replied: “That is a lie.”
after newsletter promotion
The terse exchanges between Bashir and the witness elicited several objections from prosecutor Georgina Wright, who on Wednesday said: “I object to this, your Honour. This is annoying.”
After hours of detailed questions about whether the complainant wrote a specific email about a contract more than a decade ago, Judge Glenn Walsh intervened.
“He can’t approve a contract; he is 14 years of age,” Walsh said.
The court heard one email Jones sent to A when he was 16 years of age said he had provided in excess of $100,000, “the cost is out of hand” and needs to come to an end. “Enough is enough,” he said.
The teenager replied to Jones that he and his mother could start making repayments to reimburse him. Jones wrote he did not expect to be repaid.
The witness has given evidence that he did not consent to the kiss from Jones in 2017 and that he had pulled away, saying “Enough Alan. Good night.” He said Jones “had a grin on his face”.
The incident left him scared for the consequences of pushing Jones away, he said. “I needed to be grateful, and being defiant is not being grateful and making a scene is not being grateful.”
The trial continues under Judge Walsh.

articles.title: South Korea threatens legal action if fuel shipments to Russia found to have broken law
articles.summary:
Responding to a Guardian report that revealed thousands of tonnes of fuel was transported to Russia, Seoul said it was investigating the cases

South Korea will take legal action if it finds…

blocks.text: South Korea will take legal action if it finds that shipments of fuel from its ports to Russia broke domestic law, the government has said, responding to a Guardian report on the trade.

The government, in a statement issued by the foreign and trade ministries and the customs service, said that it is “checking additional information concerning the loading cases reported by the Guardian” and “if the verification establishes that our laws and regulations have been violated, it plans to act in accordance with the law”.

Guardian analysis of port records and ship-tracking data found that in July and August over 176,000 tonnes of fuel, mostly diesel, was loaded at several South Korean ports on to seven tankers that made 14 voyages to Russia’s far east.
Three of the tankers were under UK and EU sanctions. One of them took on about 26,000 tonnes through a ship-to-ship transfer at an anchorage off the southern port of Yeosu.
Isaac Levi, an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a Finnish thinktank, said the trade “undermines the sanctions regime and South Korea’s support for Ukraine.”

Russia’s capacity to refine oil has been severely disrupted by Ukrainian drone strikes. Its refinery throughput fell in June to its lowest level in more than 20 years, and diesel output is down nearly 30% on last year, according to the International Energy Agency.

Thursday’s statement from Seoul said the refined petroleum products involved were not covered by South Korea’s export controls on Russia, which apply mainly to industrial machinery, electronics and vehicles.
“As reported by the Guardian, the loading of refined petroleum products at our ports does not constitute a violation of our domestic law”, it said.

The government said whether fuel of South Korean origin, such as diesel, had been exported “has not been confirmed”, adding that no diesel, aviation fuel or motor petrol had been “exported” from South Korea to Russia through customs clearance.
It is unclear who owned or sold the fuel, which South Korean port records do not show publicly.

The government also cautioned that the “mere fact that a vessel did not proceed directly to the final destination country stated on its declaration and instead moved to another country makes it difficult to conclude that there is a suspicion of false declaration of destination”.
It said it would examine the tankers’ actual routes, any divergence from their declared destinations and the reasons for them, before judging whether the law had been broken.
The three sanctioned tankers told South Korean authorities they were bound for Japan or Singapore before sailing to Vladivostok.

The Russian-flagged Aram Khachaturian, which is not under western sanctions, loaded at Ulsan three times in July and August and on each occasion gave a destination other than Russia before sailing there.
An adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said this week that the shipments stood in “sharp contrast” to South Korea’s sanctions policies.

On Wednesday South Korea’s presidential office said those remarks were “contrary to fact and inappropriate”, and asked Ukraine to refrain from public comment that could damage South Korea’s international credibility.
Ukraine’s foreign ministry reportedly said on Wednesday that it had raised the fuel shipments with Seoul through closed diplomatic channels and asked for an explanation.
Its spokesperson, Heorhii Tykhyi, said Kyiv also had “our own data on such activity”.

India's opposition alliance plans third day of protest against election chief

A bloc of Indian political parties, in alliance against Prime Minister Narendra Modi's BJP party, is expected to stage a protest in central Delhi on Thursday to demand the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over alleged misconduct.
Opposition leaders including Indian National Congress' Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Vadra are visibly at the forefront of the protest.

On Tuesday, Gandhi, Vadra, their supporters and over 200 allied Members of Parliament (MPs) marched on the Election Commission of India (ECI) to demand a meeting with Kumar. When blocked by the Delhi police, they began an impromptu sit in which ended with temporary detentions.

On Wednesday, the INC hosted a lunch-meeting in Delhi for about 200 MPs to discuss action against the CEC. Post lunch, they loaded up in buses to move towards the designated protest site of Jantar Mantar in central Delhi. Eventually on foot, the lawmakers were stopped by the police again.

A live feed on the YouTube channel of Gandhi's party showed police officials taking him into a vehicle and driving away. His sibling and lawmaker Vadra was also detained but taken to a different police station, as per Indian media.

"I am thankful to every INDIA alliance MP standing firm in defense of our democracy - in Parliament, outside on the streets, and today near Jantar Mantar. They can stop a march. articles.title: Pneumonic plague spread to PH highly unlikely, says health expert
articles.summary: The expert said the pneumonic plague is a treatable disease, further supporting his view that an international spread is highly unlikely.

blocks.text: October 8, 2026 | 12:04pm
An undated scanning electron microphotograph of a mass of Yersinia pestis bacteria which causes pneumonic and bubonic plague.
Wikipedia / Rocky Mountain Laboratories, NIAID, NIH

MANILA, Philippines — An infectious disease expert said that the possibility of an international spread of pneumonic plague to the Philippines is extremely low and almost bordering on zero amid widespread concerns in Russia.

Infectious disease specialist Rontgene Solante stressed on Thursday, October 8, that the Russian government has not confirmed the suspected plague, assuring that the situation should not be a cause of concern among Filipinos.

While modern air travel has the potential to spread any microbe, Solante explained that pneumonic plague is uncommon and typically occurs only in places with specific rodents or fleas that carry the bacteria that cause it.

“If I'm going to look at it this way, mukhang zero possibility na may mapupunta dito sa Pilipinas kung galing man doon ang infection. Sa tingin ko mukhang wala talaga,” Solante said in an interview with Super Radyo dzBB.
(If I’m going to look at it this way, it seems there’s a zero possibility that the infection could reach the Philippines. I don’t think there really is a possibility at all.)
A rare complication

Health concerns emerged following the death of a lab technician working in an anti-plague institute in Russia, who is suspected have died from pneumonic plague after reportedly encountering a broken test tube.
The World Health Organization (WHO) has earlier noted that the public health risk in Russia remains low and there were no signs of an outbreak detected.
According to Solante, the pneumonic plague caused by the Yersinia pestis bacterium is a rare, more severe form of the bubonic plague affecting the lungs.
It can be transmitted from person to person through respiratory droplets, unlike the bubonic plague, that are typically spread via flea bites.
The pneumonic plague produces symptoms similar to other types of pneumonia, including fever, cough, and difficulty breathing.
“Ang difference lang nito, masyadong progressive ang pneumonia nito kaya nga mataas ang mortality. That's why it's so rare but it's also very fatal,” Solante said.
(Its only difference is that it has a more progressive pneumonia, which is why it has more mortality. That’s why it’s so rare but it’s also very fatal.)
A treatable disease
Solante said the pneumonic plague is a treatable disease, further supporting his view that an international spread is highly unlikely.
The specialist explained that there are existing medications that are considered highly effective in treating pneumonic plague, making the situation even easier to control.
The Russian health authorities are also currently conducting tests, quarantines, and other necessary measures to address the plague concerns, according to Solante.
“This is something also that's treatable. Mukhang malabo ang in terms of international spread,” the expert said. (It seems it’s unlikely in terms of international spread.)

articles.title: Japan beer giants raided over suspicions they colluded to set the price of beverages
articles.summary:
Investigators probe Asahi, Kirin, Suntory and Sapporo breweries – which together control more than 90% of Japan’s beer market

Japanese authorities have raided the country’s four biggest…

blocks.text: Japanese authorities have raided the country’s four biggest breweries over suspicions they colluded to set the price of beer and other beverages – a practice media reports said could have forced drinkers to pay over the odds.

Officials from the Fair Trade Commission this week searched the offices of Asahi Breweries, Kirin Brewery, Suntory Beer and Sapporo Breweries – which together control more than 90% of the domestic market. The quartet are suspected of violating the anti-monopoly law.
The commission’s secretary general, Hiroo Iwanari, confirmed an investigation had begun, but declined to give details. The companies said they would cooperate with authorities.

The commission is understood to have launched the investigation given the potential effect the alleged cartel has had on prices after wholesalers sell their products on to supermarkets, convenience stores, bars and restaurants, the Mainichi Shimbun said.

Japanese media quoted sources as saying that sales managers and other executives from the breweries were suspected of meeting secretly over a prolonged period to coordinate on the timing and scale of retail price increases, which ranged from several yen to several dozen yen a time.

Prices for beer and a low-malt version called happoshu have risen multiple times to reflect the rising cost of raw materials and logistics. The commission suspects the breweries bypassed proper pricing competition and collaborated to ensure they made a profit, the Mainichi said.

Alcohol consumption in Japan has declined in recent decades as a result of depopulation and changes in drinking habits among younger people. But sales still reached ¥3.8tn ($24.3bn) in 2024, with beer accounting for 30% of the total, followed by happoshu and third-category beer, which contains little or no malt, with a combined 11.9%

The four breweries have all raised their prices at the same time, most recently in April last year, citing the rising cost of materials and distribution. Prices also rose in October 2022 and October 2023.
Shares in Asahi, Kirin, Suntory and Sapporo fell after Wednesday’s raids – the first investigation of its kind involving the food and beverage industry.

Japanese media quoted sources as saying the commission had judged the case to be particularly serious given its potential impact on consumers, adding that the probe could result in a criminal complaint.
The probe comes three months after the commission raided six Japanese ice-cream makers over allegations of operating a cartel.

articles.title: Indonesia accused of ‘gross negligence’ in wildfires lawsuit as haze tests region
articles.summary:
NGOs in Indonesian Borneo file class action lawsuit calling for government to better manage annual fires and

The Indonesian government has been accused of “gross negligence” in a class…
articles.byline: Oliver Holmes in Bangkok and agencies

blocks.text: The Indonesian government has been accused of “gross negligence” in a class action lawsuit over its handling of wildfires that have cloaked large parts of South-east Asia in a toxic haze, shuttered schools and caused a spike in respiratory illnesses.

The lawsuit, filed by indigenous and civil society groups in the Indonesian part of Borneo, named President Prabowo Subianto and the governor of West Kalimantan among 10 defendants. The case seeks comprehensive recovery and rehabilitation measures that would include covering the healthcare costs of residents.
None of those named in the lawsuit attended the opening day of court in West Kalimantan’s provincial capital Pontianak on Wednesday, leading judges to adjourn the hearing until 21 October.

“We feel sad and regretful about their absence … But on the other hand, we also understand that perhaps this haze condition caused them to be unable to land in Pontianak,” the plaintiffs’ lawyer, Glorio Sanen, told reporters.
Sanen said the case was “a step to address the problem” of wildfires that flare up annually in Indonesia, where they are often lit as a cheap way to clear land for oil palm planting.

Indonesia, the world’s largest producer of palm oil, has been accused of not doing enough to stop the so-called “slash and burn” land clearances, although the government has vowed a crackdown and deployed the military to fight the fires.

The blazes hit a crisis point this year due to an unusually intense El Niño weather phenomenon, which has created drier-than-usual conditions, sending a putrid smog to Malaysia, Brunei and Singapore, and even the Philippines.

The transboundary haze has angered Indonesia’s neighbours. Schools in the Malaysian state of Johor, just north of Singapore, were to be closed on Thursday and Friday due to deteriorating air quality, local authorities said.
The four plaintiffs in the West Kalimantan lawsuit, which was filed last month, include a chapter of Indigenous NGO AMAN and the local branch of Catholic ​Youth.

Yakobus Kumis, a plaintiff representing a Dayak ethnic group, indigenous to the island of Borneo, expressed disappointment that government representatives did not attend this week’s hearing, saying it was a “way of the central government teaching the people that violating the law is OK.”
He said the government ignored warning signs ahead of the fires breaking out, and called for the smoke crisis to be classified as a national disaster.
A similar lawsuit filed last year at a court in South Sumatra was dismissed.
The presidential office did not immediately ⁠respond to a request for comment.
Agence France-Presse and Reuters contributed to this report

articles.title: Veteran Indian actor Nana Patekar dies at 75
articles.summary: Known for his intense performances, Patekar carved out a distinctive place in Indian cinema.

blocks.text: Veteran Indian actor Nana Patekar, known for his intense performances and distinct dialogue delivery, has died at the age of 75 in Goa, his son Malhar told the BBC.

One of the most recognisable faces of Indian cinema, Patekar won three National Film Awards and became known for playing complex, often volatile characters in films such as Parinda, Krantiveer and Ab Tak Chhappan. He was also a prominent figure in Marathi language cinema and theatre.
He was rushed to hospital after being found unconscious at his home in Goa in the early hours of Thursday.
"Despite 45 minutes of continuous CPR, he could not be revived," Dr Shekhar Salkar of Manipal Hospital in Goa told ANI news agency.

Patekar made his debut with the film Gaman in 1978 and continued to play smaller roles in several films. But the intensity that he brought on the screen was hard to miss and soon he landed a role in Parinda in 1989, making him a household name across India. His portrayal of the volatile, gritty gangster Anna won him his first National Film Award and the Filmfare Award.

He didn't look back after this and played many memorable characters in several films through the 1990s. The range of the characters he played showcased the depth of his acting talent and mastery over his craft.

His portrayal of Major Chauhan in Prahaar – a film he also directed – won him praise. Then there was the villainous character of Majid Khan in Angaar, the patriotic firebrand of Tirangaa, and, most notably, Pratap Narayan Tilak in Krantiveer, for which he won the national award for best actor.
Just when critics thought that playing loud characters was his mainstay, he proved them wrong by delivering a mesmerising performance in Khamoshi as a person who could not hear or speak.
Director Prakash Jha's Rajneeti in 2010 added another dimension to his acting as his portrayal of an astute politician was delivered with perfection.

The breadth of Patekar's career showcases the depth of his talent. He has played gangsters, soldiers, policemen, politicians, patriots, villains, comic characters and tragic figures, while moving between Hindi and Marathi cinema and sometimes also working behind the camera as a director and writer.
His three national awards for Parinda, Krantiveer and Agni Sakshi are a testament to his career.

Patekar was also an influential figure in both Marathi and Hindi theatre. Before cinema made him a familiar face, he spent years working in theatre, where he developed the intensity and discipline that would become hallmarks of his screen performances.
Purush and Hamidabai Chi Kothi were two of his most famous plays. Despite being successful in films, he remained active in theatre throughout his professional life.
