articles.title: France's school protests: what lies behind the anger
articles.summary: Students' blockades and marches spring from real grievances – and from France's habit of settling policy on the street.

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Since late September students across France have been holding protests against underfunding in education, and have been blocking access to many high schools.

The movement has turned violent in places – hundreds of students, teachers and police officers have been injured. Thousands of people – including an unknown number of outside troublemakers – have been arrested.
The protesters are complaining about staff shortages and dilapidated facilities in the country's lycées, schools which are attended by 15-18-year-olds.

"Sometimes our teachers are absent for several weeks without being replaced," Madalena, a Paris student, told the BBC on Tuesday as demonstrations brought out hundreds of thousands across France . Her school buildings, she added, were "boiling hot" during the recent heat waves.

There is a variety of other complaints. Some resent the banning of mobile phones or school days that last until 18:00. "You get home at 7 pm, and have no time to sleep or do your homework," one lycéen told France 2.
France's online platform that allocates places in higher education, Parcoursup, is another sore point.

The frustration has deep roots. About 80% of each cohort now passes the baccalauréat, which entitles students to a university place - though not necessarily their preferred choice. This leads to a scramble for desirable courses, and an anxiety focused on Parcoursup, which many regard as opaque.
Watch: Riot police clash with school protesters and use tear gas on Tuesday
Those grievances are real. But do they by themselves explain the form the protest movement has taken? How does France compare with other countries?
According to a recent report by the OECD, a club of developed nations, the French government spends more per lycée student than the EU average for upper-secondary schools.
Teacher shortages are indeed acute, but no worse than elsewhere. By OECD measures they are actually milder – fewer posts go unfilled – although French teachers receive relatively low pay.

Schooldays that stretch into the late afternoon are indeed a problem for French pupils. This is the result mostly of long lunch breaks and complex schedules rather than making up for holidays, which are not especially long compared with other EU countries.
The extended day has always been a sad fact of French school life and can hardly account for the present eruption. Neither can pressure created by a dysfunctional higher-education system.
In most European countries, 80-90% of young people complete secondary education, and competition for good university places creates stress elsewhere too.

And while underfunding, dilapidated buildings and fears about the future are behind the students' discontent, those complaints do not by themselves explain why the movement has become "unprecedented" in terms of the number of schools, pupils and the degree of violence involved, in the words of Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez.

blocks.caption: Image caption, About 500 people were arrested during Tuesday's unrest

blocks.text: Image source, EPA
About 500 people were arrested during Tuesday's unrest
The scale of protests is all the more remarkable as those involved are taking considerable risks.

Blockading a school or university by threats or force is illegal, and draws in police, as well as casseurs (vandals), and pupils have become caught up in police crowd-control operations that are often heavy handed.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, in his latest message, has insisted security forces are not under orders to "confront high-school students", only to enforce the law.

To understand the pupils' tactics, one must look beyond the barricaded school gates to a political tradition. In France, the power has often resided on the street as much as in elected bodies. Students know this as well as anyone else.

In October 1990, a rape at a school in Seine-Saint-Denis – an area north of Paris that has been a focus for the present unrest – was the trigger for mass rallies against underfunding and staff shortages. It resulted in the government releasing the equivalent of €1.2bn (£1bn) in today's money for lycées.
In October 1998, 500,000 pupils marched across France over similar demands, resulting in almost €1bn to renovate schools and 14,000 extra staff.
On several occasions student protests defeated government reforms – such as a university overhaul in 1986 and a lower youth minimum wage in 1994.
Why has France suspended the use of stun grenades on protesters?
Probably the most striking display of student power came in 2006, with the withdrawal of a law designed to loosen hire-and-fire rules for those under 26 to try to tackle youth unemployment.
The measure, passed by parliament and signed by then-President Jacques Chirac, was scrapped after weeks of blockades in universities and lycées often marred by violence.
French adults have shown how blockading roads can prevail over elected officials.

The gilets jaunes (yellow vests) uprising of 2018-2019 – which saw shops ransacked and government buildings attacked across the country – led the government to drop a rise in fuel taxes and approve €10bn in spending.
The street does not always win.

In 1968 – a heroic precedent cited by every French protest movement – a student uprising was actually brought to an end by election. But the lycéens are heirs to a political culture in which demonstrators compete with elected officials to be seen as the legitimate voice of the people.
On the face of it, the current balance of power favour the pupils. A poll for BMFTV suggests that that 72% of French people regard their demands as legitimate and 55% support the movement.
Backed by many teachers, labour unions and left-wing politicians, the protesters are on the front foot. Another rally is planned for Thursday afternoon.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Lecornu will find it difficult to open the purse strings

blocks.text: Lecornu will find it difficult to open the purse strings

The government, by contrast, has never been weaker. After nine years in power, Emmanuel Macron is a deeply unpopular lame duck, barred from standing in the presidential election due in six months' time.

His decision to call a snap election in June 2024 has resulted in a hopelessly gridlocked assembly. Lecornu has described himself as the "weakest prime minister" in living memory and seems unlikely to get a budget through parliament.

But that very weakness could prove an asset in his showdown with students. Faced with rising borrowing costs, a deficit of 5.4% of GDP and a public debt at its highest level since the 1940s, Lecornu is financially as well as politically hamstrung.
Unlike his predecessors under intense pressure from the street, he has nothing to give.

articles.title: Three people killed in Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia airports, officials say
articles.summary: The Houthis have claimed responsibility for the attacks, which mark an escalation in the conflict.

blocks.text: Three people have been killed in attacks on Saudi Arabia airports over two days, authorities said, as flare-up of fighting spilled across the Yemen border into the kingdom.
Two people were killed and 28 wounded in an attack at Abha International Airport, Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation (Gaca) said in a statement on Wednesday.
In a separate incident, one person was killed and eight were wounded in an attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia's capital, it added.
The attacks, which the Houthis have claimed responsibility for, mark an escalation in the renewed war between the Saudi-backed government forces and the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen.
The two airports were attacked on 6 and 7 October, according to Gaca, which did not specify when each airport was hit.
Two women, of Moroccan and Algerian nationalities, were killed during the Abha airport attack, near the Yemen border, according to Gaca.
Meanwhile, a male resident of Sudanese nationality was killed at King Khalid airport, it added.

The country's civil aviation authority did not name who was responsible for the attacks, but Houthi military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said its armed forces had attacked both Saudi Arabia airports with ballistic missiles and drones.

The Houthi military spokesperson also said the Houthis attacked Aden's International Airport in Yemen on Wednesday. The airport is a main international gateway for parts of Yemen outside of Houthi control and has been repeatedly targeted when fighting erupts in the country.
Saree said the two attacks on Saudi Arabia's airports were in "response to the Saudi aggression against our country" which saw "60 airstrikes and missile attacks in the past 24 hours".

The civil war in Yemen has worsened in recent weeks, after the Houthis, who control most of the country's north-west, seized strategically important stretches of the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive.
That included the port of Mokha on the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which is the narrowest point of the Red Sea and a chokepoint for global shipping.
But Yemeni pro-government forces backed by Saudi Arabia have since said they had "secured" the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea.
They also declared an all out war in an effort to take all territory held by the Houthis.
In a statement issued late on Wednesday, the official spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition said the Houthis' attacks on Saudi Arabia's airports "will not go unpunished".
The spokesperson said the Saudi coalition had targeted more than 80 Houthi military sites across "governorates of Saada, Al Hudaydah, Al Jawf and Ma'rib".
The Saudi-led coalition formed in 2015 after Arab countries joined forces to stop the Houthis taking over Yemen from the country's internationally recognised government.

A temporary ceasefire was brokered in 2022 after years of air strikes and ground fighting led to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people, triggering one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres has condemned "the continued Houthi cross-border attacks" on Saudi Arabia and said he was "deeply concerned by the sharp escalation in fighting".
Hundreds of people have reportedly been killed on both sides since the latest Houthis' advance.
The UN said on Wednesday more than 200,000 people have been displaced by the escalation.

articles.title: US: Award-winning Kashmiri filmmaker detained
articles.summary: Arfat Sheikh was detained by ICE agents in Washington on September 24, it was confirmed on Wednesday. Officials say he "illegally overstayed his lawful admittance" as US President Trump pursues an…

image.caption: Friends and relatives say Arfat Sheikh's detention by ICE agents is 'unlawful' and are calling for his release [FILE: May 26, 2026]Image: Charly Triballeau/AFP

blocks.text: A filmmaker whose award-winning work has explored conflict in his native Kashmir has been detained by United States immigration officials on suspicion of residing and working in the country illegally.

Arfat Sheikh was detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) after disembarking a flight from California at Washington Dulles International Airport on September 24, according to a statement from friends and relatives who labeled his detention "unlawful" and are calling for his release.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, confirmed to the Reuters news agency on Wednesday that Sheikh had "legally entered the US on a temporary basis and illegally overstayed his lawful admittance."
Sheikh, 42, entered the US in 2019 on a student visa and enrolled on a graduate course in film studies at Georgia State University, according to the statement from friends and family.
Having applied for asylum in 2020, the statement said he had a ​pending immigration application and was authorized to work and live in the US. It did not mention the ground for asylum.
The DHS said Sheikh would receive due process but that a pending ​application does not confer legal residency status.
ICE arrests up amid Trump immigration crackdown
US President Donald Trump has been pursuing an immigration crackdown and deportation drive that he claims is aimed at improving domestic security.

His administration said in August it was to "identify ⁠and revoke the non-immigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the US claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently."
The number of ICE arrests hit record levels this summer, with about 51,000 recorded across August.

Critics say the crackdown has violated due process and ​free speech rights and ​has created an unsafe ⁠environment, particularly for ethnic minorities, who have raised concerns about racial profiling.
ICE targets South Asians for removal from United States
Sheikh, who hails from India-administered Kashmir, won the Emerging Filmmaker Activist Award at the Teaneck International Film Festival in 2025.

His first feature film, 2024's "Saffron Kingdom," won Best Feature Film at the Chicago Filmmakers Awards, ​the LA Film and Documentary Awards, the Melbourne Independent Film Festival and the ​Wake Forest ⁠Film Festival.
The film explored conflict in Kashmir, a disputed Muslim-majority region claimed by both Hindu-majority India and Islamic Pakistan, which each control only part of it and have fought wars over it.

articles.title: Texas carries out first US execution since Christa Pike's botched lethal injections
articles.summary: Lawyers for Jamaal Howard had asked a judge to pause the execution after Christa Pike's botched lethal injections.

blocks.text: A death row inmate was executed by lethal injection on Wednesday evening in Texas, the first execution in the US since the failed attempt to put Christa Pike to death last week.
Lawyers for 46-year-old Jamaal Howard had asked a judge to pause the execution in light of Pike's botched injections last week, according to the BBC's US partner, CBS News.
But courts denied their requests, and he received a fatal dose of pentobarbital at the state prison in Huntsville. He was pronounced dead at 20:03 local time.
Howard was convicted and sentenced to death for the 2000 murder of a convenience store clerk during a robbery he committed.

His lawyers had argued that because Texas planned to inject Howard with the same drug - pentobarbital - that was used on Pike, he faced the same risks. They also alleged that Texas' supply of the drug had become degraded, as Pike's lawyers have similarly argued.
A court twice denied their appeals and the US Supreme Court also turned down the appeal late Wednesday.
"Texas should not be eager to follow in Tennessee's footsteps; a stay would keep that from happening," Howard's attorneys had argued, CBS reported.

Howard's attorneys also asked Texas Governor Greg Abbott, a Republican, to delay the execution by 30 days so they could seek additional information about the drug used in the execution. The governor did not grant the delay.
Howard was 20 when he shot Vickie Swartout, 42, who was working at a convenience store in Texas. Howard stole a carton of cigarettes and $114 from the register.
Asked if he had a final statement before his execution, Howard apologized to Swartout's family, who watched from a witness room, US media report.
"I wish that you accept my apology, and I wish for your forgiveness," Howard said. "I'm sorry for what happened. I wish you can learn to forgive me one of these days."

articles.title: Trump wants a new Camp David retreat at his posh Florida golf club
articles.summary: Trump's estate would stand in stark contrast to the rustic Camp David and mark another tradition transformed by Trump.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
President Trump gestures before boarding Marine One departs after a Cabinet meeting at Camp David on 31 July 2026 in Thurmont, Maryland.
ByBernd Debusmann and Sareen Habeshian
US President Donald Trump is looking to create a presidential retreat similar to Camp David at his Florida golf club.
The club would foot constructions costs as a "gift" to Americans and provide free memberships to future presidents - and accommodations to visiting foreign dignitaries.
"It's only about two minutes away from the airport … and they could spend the weekend there, like a retreat, like a sort of Camp David retreat," Trump said on Wednesday.

If it comes to fruition, Trump's transformed golf estate would stand in stark contrast to the rustic Camp David, once a Great Depression-era camp in the woods for federal employees. It would also mark another tradition transformed by Trump.

blocks.caption: Image caption, A view of the Trump International Golf Club in West Palm Beach, Florida.

blocks.text: A view of the Trump International Golf Club in West Palm Beach, Florida.

The US president has sought to cement his legacy through changes to the White House, including gilded gold leaf accents in the Oval Office, demolition of the East Wing and construction of a ballroom. He is pushing ahead with plans to erect a massive triumphal arch elsewhere in Washington.

He has hosted national security meetings and other events at Camp David, known as the president's country residence. The Camp David property - set deep in Catoctin Mountain Park in Frederick County, Maryland - was first taken over as a retreat by President Franklin Roosevelt, who nicknamed it "Shangri-La".

The area is rustic, and in some ways resembles the military facility it officially is - Naval Support Facility, Thurmont. The entire facility is staffed by uniformed members of the US Navy and Marine Corps.

blocks.caption: Image caption, US President Joe Biden, center, greets Fumio Kishida, Japan's prime minister, right, and Yoon Suk Yeol, South Korea's president, left, during a trilateral summit at Camp David in 2023.

blocks.text: US President Joe Biden, center, greets Fumio Kishida, Japan's prime minister, right, and Yoon Suk Yeol, South Korea's president, left, during a trilateral summit at Camp David in 2023.

The secure facility is largely hidden from public view, with Marines guarding the perimeter and airspace above restricted. It is not marked on maps of the national park, even if its location is known to locals.
Press is only very rarely allowed on the grounds - meaning that photography of the wood and stone cabins and lodges that make up most of the facility are tightly controlled.

On a recent visit by the BBC, for example, reporters in the White House press pool were under strict instructions to avoid taking images in unauthorized areas or providing details on the camp's layout.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Then-US President Barack Obama (L) meets with Eurozone leaders on the Laurel Cabin patio during the G8 Summit on in 2012 at Camp David.

blocks.text: Then-US President Barack Obama (L) meets with Eurozone leaders on the Laurel Cabin patio during the G8 Summit on in 2012 at Camp David.

Trump International Golf Club in West Palm Beach, on the other hand, is connected to the rest of the city by ample roadways, some of which are lined with supporters or protesters when the president is there.

The 27-hole golf course and club bills itself as having "a lively social scene" and fine dining - and is visited often by Trump's political allies during his many weekends in Florida. It includes a luxurious clubhouse, a gift store and hosts frequent social events for members.

The president's argument that the area is "secure" is notable. In recent months, Trump has frequently used national security and safety arguments to justify various projects in Washington DC, including his White House ballroom project the planned Triumphal Arch.

Asked by reporters if he would call the new presidential retreat at his golf club "Camp Donald", Trump replied, "Well, it's already called Trump International. It's one of the best golf courses in the world."
He said among advantages is the absence of high buildings and homes looming "so you don't have ... people hiding behind windows".
"They can get maximum safety," the president said. "It's a great idea and it'll be used a lot."

blocks.caption: Image caption, The entrance driveway at Trump International Golf Club in Palm Beach County, Florida

blocks.text: The entrance driveway at Trump International Golf Club in Palm Beach County, Florida
Trump said at the Oval Office on Wednesday that Secret Service officials first suggested the idea of using the golf club as a presidential retreat, and that he thinks it is "a great idea".
"It's about as safe as they could possibly get," he said.
The BBC has contacted the Secret Service for comment.

A letter dated 3 September from the golf course's attorney to the county commission in Florida said Trump offered to deem the club as a "U.S. Presidential Golf Course" for presidents and visiting heads of state, according to USA TODAY's Palm Beach Post.
The letter, obtained by the local outlet, states that the golf club would provide access to all its facilities at "no cost to the federal government" and provide free membership to future presidents.
The golf club would front constructions costs as a "gift" to Americans and local residents, according to the letter.
"This wouldn't be for me," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on Wednesday. "This would be for all future presidents."

articles.title: Marcos arrives in Singapore for investment, regional talks
articles.summary: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. arrived in Singapore late Wednesday, October 7, for a five-day working visit to promote investment opportunities in the Philippines and discuss regional issues with…

blocks.text: October 8, 2026 | 10:47am

MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. arrived in Singapore late Wednesday, October 7, for a five-day working visit to promote investment opportunities in the Philippines and discuss regional issues with Singaporean officials.
The presidential plane landed at Changi Airport at 11:05 p.m.
Marcos is scheduled to attend the 24th Forbes Global CEO Conference, which will bring together around 450 business and thought leaders from around the world.
He said he would promote the Philippines as an investment destination for digital technology, artificial intelligence (AI), advanced manufacturing and other growth sectors.

“This time, our economic engagement will have a broader global focus. I will present the opportunities that the Philippines offers in digital technology, AI, and advanced manufacturing,” Marcos said in a departure statement posted on his Facebook.
He will also highlight opportunities in infrastructure, energy, healthcare and other sectors.
Marcos said his visit builds on his trip to Singapore in July, when he met with investors in digital infrastructure, AI, healthcare and other priority sectors.

But the president said attracting investments would not be enough, as the Philippines would also need to develop the infrastructure, energy capacity and technical expertise required by emerging industries.
“As we pursue these ambitions, we must also prepare for the economy we are building,” Marcos said.
“AI, data centers, advanced manufacturing, and other emerging industries will require greater amounts of reliable, affordable, and sustainable energy,” he added.
Marcos is also scheduled to visit the Singapore Nuclear Research and Safety Institute upon the invitation of Temasek Foundation and Ayala Corp.
He will learn about Singapore’s experience in developing scientific and technical capabilities in nuclear technology and safety.

“The Philippines must continue to examine all viable options for our long-term energy security, while developing the knowledge and capabilities needed to make sound decisions for our future,” Marcos said.
The president will also meet with Singapore Prime Minister and Minister for Finance Lawrence Wong to discuss bilateral relations and regional developments.
Singapore will assume the Association of Southeast Asian Nations chairship next year, following the Philippines’ 2026 chairship.
Marcos said he would discuss with Wong ways to sustain and advance regional priorities.
“I return to Singapore with a clear purpose: to build on one of our most important economic partnerships and prepare our country for the industries of the future,” the president said.

articles.title: IMF reaches tentative $1.21 billion bailout deal with Pakistan
articles.summary: Pakistan's dependence on Gulf energy imports, remittances and regional financing has left the economy exposed to the fallout from the Middle East conflict.

image.caption: Pakistan has seen soaring prices in recent months that threatened an already fragile economy [FILE: July 16, 2019]Image: Akhtar Soomro/REUTERS

blocks.text: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has reached a staff-level agreement with Pakistan that could unlock about $1.21 billion (roughly €1 billion) in financing, the lender said on Wednesday, as the South Asian country grapples with spiking food and fuel prices, and high unemployment.
The bailout deal still needs to be approved by the IMF Executive Board.
IMF negotiator Iva Petrova said Pakistan had successfully navigated the impact of the Middle East conflict, with strong policies helping preserve macroeconomic stability.
How does the Middle East conflict impact Pakistan?
Pakistan's economy grew 4% in the first three quarters of fiscal 2026 with full-year growth estimated at 3.6%, the IMF said.
Petrova attributed the weakened momentum to "higher energy prices and supply disruptions."
Inflation eased to about 10.3% in September after peaking in May, while core inflation remained contained, Petrova said.
Pakistan remains dependent on external financing to shore up foreign exchange reserves and meet debt repayments.

A prolonged Middle East conflict makes it particularly vulnerable due to its dependence on Gulf energy imports, remittances and financing from the region, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence economist Ahmad Mobeen earlier this year.
In the recent past, Pakistan has had to turn to the IMF to tackle Islamabad's acute balance-of-payments crisis.

articles.title: Woman at centre of Cornell gang-rape case was 'misled' about investigation, lawyer says
articles.summary: The woman who says several men raped her at a Cornell University fraternity party was "misled" about the status of the criminal investigation in the weeks after she went to police, her lawyer said…

image.caption: Cornell's police department gave the woman at the centre of gang-rape allegations the impression that a criminal investigation was continuing, her lawyer says — but the criminal inquiry ended almost as soon as it began. (Matt Burkhartt/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

The woman who says several men raped her at a Cornell University fraternity party was "misled" about the status of the criminal investigation in the weeks after she went to police, her lawyer said Wednesday.
Criminal inquiry ended almost as soon as it began, but Jane Doe was given impression it was ongoing: lawyer

Even as she took her allegations about a 2024 gang rape at the Chi Phi fraternity house through Cornell's internal disciplinary process, the university's police department gave her the impression that a criminal investigation was continuing, lawyer Thomas Giuffra told The Associated Press.
In fact, the criminal inquiry ended almost as soon as it began.

Tompkins County district attorney Matthew Van Houten, the local prosecutor, made the decision not to go forward with a criminal case within days of the woman giving her first substantial interviews to police.

items: Allegations in Cornell 7 case fit pattern of institutional failure on sexual assault, says sociologist

blocks.text: Van Houten has said he asked Cornell's police department to convey the decision to the woman, who is referred to in court documents as Jane Doe, but never spoke personally to her or her lawyer.
Giuffra said the woman was told the criminal investigation was ongoing.
"I think she was misled," he said. "I was involved with this case early on. I thought they were still investigating. It was news to me that they weren't doing anything."
At the time, Giuffra added, he assumed investigators just needed more time to speak with witnesses and build a case.
"But nothing was being done, and we didn't know that," he said.
A messages seeking comment was left for Van Houten. Cornell's media relations office, citing pending litigation, declined to comment on behalf of the university's police department.

The district attorney said in a statement last week that he was confident no further investigation was necessary after prosecutors and criminal investigators from his office reviewed a six-page summary of the woman's account, written by a police officer.
'Cornell 7' lawsuit: What we know
Different accounts
Based on that summary, Van Houten said he believed no crime had been committed, and that the woman's participation in drug use and sex was "voluntary, conscious and consensual."

That description differs sharply with what the woman told police and university investigators, and with what she alleged in a lawsuit filed against seven Chi Phi fraternity members, Cornell and others last month.

Among other things, Giuffra said, the six-page report omitted the woman telling investigators, "I can say with 100 per cent confidence I was raped," that she was subjected to physical violence, and that a fraternity brother had sent a message to a group chat using a vulgar term to advertise that a woman's body was freely available.

Last week, citing investigative records it obtained, the New York Times reported that a Cornell police investigator tried to get Van Houten's office to consider additional evidence in the weeks after the alleged rape, but was rebuffed.
"At first I thought these police were incompetent," Giuffra said. "It sounds like they were doing the right thing. And they just got shut down."

Giuffra said while he and Jane Doe have received death threats, he has been heartened by an outpouring of support — including rallies and protests on the Cornell campus and more than 1,000 women who have emailed him to share anger, frustration, solidarity and stories of their own assaults.
Cornell students protest university handling of sexual assault case
Case taken away from Van Houten

Jane Doe, who was a student in 2024, alleges that Chi Phi members plied her with alcohol and drugs and several of them sexually assaulted her. One man sent others a message inviting them to participate, according to a lawsuit she filed last month.

Lawyers for two of the men have denied they participated in a sexual assault. Attempts by The Associated Press to reach the others or their representatives have been unsuccessful. Some of the men who underwent a university disciplinary hearing in 2024 told investigators that the sexual activity was consensual or said they were not involved.

The woman went to Cornell police in November 2024, though no criminal charges resulted. In the wake of her lawsuit, Van Houten said he was reopening the investigation. Days later, Gov. Kathy Hochul took the case away from him and appointed the state's attorney general, Letitia James, as a special prosecutor.

items: Jane Doe at centre of Cornell rape case targeted with threats, her lawyer says
Cornell taps ex-Justice Department official Sally Yates to review school's handling of sexual assault cases

blocks.text: Giuffra applauded the move, saying he was troubled by Van Houten's plan for conducting the reopened investigation and "didn't think he was up to the task."
Giuffra said the district attorney wanted to take the case to a grand jury and have Jane Doe testify before the panel within two weeks.

That timeline, leaving little time to review evidence or interview witnesses, suggested Van Houten may have been trying "to go take a dive and not really give it his best effort and not do any investigation," Giuffra said.
James hasn't said how long her investigation might take, but suggested it could be months.

On Wednesday, one of the men named in Jane Doe's lawsuit filed a court petition seeking James's removal from the case, arguing she showed bias by posting on social media a few days before her appointment: "What this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable."
A spokesperson for James declined to comment.
Cornell closed down the Chi Phi campus chapter in 2024 and says it expelled some students and suspended others after an investigation under the federal Title IX law.

This week Cornell trustees brought in former U.S. deputy attorney general Sally Yates to review how the school investigates sexual assault and sexual harassment, how the disciplinary process works, the campus police response and more.

blocks.text: The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.
On this page, we bring you the latest updates, analyses, videos, and photos as the trial of the Vice President unfolds.

articles.title: Jurors in Beau Lamarre-Condon murder case shown photos of decomposed bodies
articles.summary:
Former NSW police officer has pleaded not guilty to the February 2024 murders of Jesse Baird and Luke Davies in Sydney

  • Get our

blocks.text: Photographs of the decomposed bodies of Jesse Baird and Luke Davies have been shown to 15 jurors tasked with deciding whether the two men were murdered.
Former police officer Beau Lamarre-Condon, 31, has pleaded not guilty to the February 2024 murders of Baird, 26, and Davies, 29.
The third week of his double murder trial has pivoted to how investigators found the remains in rural NSW.

Retired crime scene officer Greg Moon, who coordinated the forensic sweep of the Greek monastery at Bungonia where the men’s bodies were found, continued giving evidence on Thursday about the condition of the remains.
Most of the family members of Baird, a former TV presenter, and Davies, a Qantas flight attendant, have not been present in court for the grisly forensic evidence.
Justice Natalie Adams warned jurors on Thursday they would see confronting photos of decomposition.
The bodies were discovered inside two surfboard or stand-up paddleboard bags, with the smaller bag containing the body zipped up inside a larger one, Moon said.
Moon said the bodies were discovered one on top of the other with rocks and small branches placed on top.

blocks.caption: Evidence and testimony in week two of Beau Lamarre-Condon’s trial – video

blocks.text: Fellow investigator Christine Abela said she immediately knew something was amiss when she first arrived at the rural property more than a week after the two men were killed in the summer of 2024.
“There was a strong smell as soon as I got out of the car,” she told a NSW supreme court jury on Wednesday.
“The scent of a decomposing body.”
Abela detailed how investigators found concrete blocks, a gym weight and a cut padlock at Cella Farm, where Lamarre-Condon allegedly unsuccessfully attempted to sink the bodies in a dam.
after newsletter promotion
Moon said there were multiple indicators that the remains had been at the monastery, about 20km away from the farm, for several days.
“A large number of maggots and other insects were present in the bags along with other decompositional fluids,” he said.
Lamarre-Condon’s efforts to clean up and dispose of Baird and Davies’ bodies have come under scrutiny during the trial.
His barrister says the actions to dispose of their bodies at Bungonia, 200km south of Sydney, were indicative of his panic about the unexpected deaths.

Earlier in the trial, jurors were shown CCTV of the alleged actions the senior constable took in the hours after the killings, including buying a second surfboard bag and hiring a larger second vehicle.
The footage, released by the court on Thursday, allegedly shows the heavily disguised Lamarre-Condon returning to the alleged murder scene laden down with cleaning products and a tarpaulin.
The 12-week trial continues.

articles.title: Sara Duterte trial recap, Oct. 7: VP and husband's millions
articles.summary: A record-breaking fifteen executives from banks and insurers took the witness stand in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on Wednesday, October 7, to authenticate documents that…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — A record-breaking fifteen executives from banks and insurers took the witness stand in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on Wednesday, October 7, to authenticate documents that attest to her and her husband's alleged wealth.

Article II charges Duterte with amassing wealth disproportionate to her lawful income and failing to fully and truthfully disclose her and her husband Manases Carpio’s assets in her SALNs (statements of assets, liabilities and net worth) for 2022, 2023 and 2024.
It also accuses her of failing to divest from businesses, as the Constitution requires of the president and vice president.

In calling the bank and insurance witnesses, the prosecution sought to put on record the year-end balances in the couple’s accounts, so it can compare each year’s balance against the SALN for the same year.
Prosecutors have argued the records are meant to establish a baseline of Duterte’s wealth and a “pattern of non-disclosure.”

The marathon hearing on Wednesday laid out two clashing ways of reading Duterte’s finances. It's the prosecution's argument that there are serious indications of undeclared wealth just by comparing the SALN and bank balances alone. Citing bank records, the prosecution has pointed out that the Duterte couple had P59 million in bank balances at the end of 2022, her first year in office, against P13.325 million in declared “other personal properties.”

The defense, meanwhile, has countered that transactions from before she took office are irrelevant and that not all the transactions being wielded as evidence by the prosecution were signed off by Duterte herself.
Duterte and her husband have more than 30 to 40 total bank accounts across eight different banks, according to the prosecution.
Here are the three highlights from the proceedings on October 7.
1. The ‘tinikling’ manager’s checks

A bank executive told the court that P41.7 million from a time deposit in the names of Sara Duterte and her father, former president Rodrigo Duterte, was repeatedly moved into bank-issued checks in 2011.

Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI) division head Marvin Galvez testified that the money started as a P40.65-million time deposit opened in January 2010. By March 9, 2011, the amount had matured to P41.72 million after the interest had accumulated during several rollover periods. On this day, the funds were moved to the Dutertes' joint account at BPI’s Julia Vargas branch.

The same day, the full amount was used to buy a manager’s check, a check guaranteed by the bank and valid for six months. After that check lapsed, another for the same amount was bought on Oct. 20, 2011.

Upon questioning, Galvez confirmed that money held in a manager’s check leaves the depositor’s account but does not appear in the year-end balance. Instead, it is moved into the bank's internal settlement account, making it the bank's liability.

Because of this, prosecutors pointed to the checks as a way of bypassing the SALN by keeping the money in limbo, given public officials are required to declare their cash on hand or in bank, among others, when they file the document by the end of each year.
Private prosecutor James Bryan Alih said the money moved this way for “three or four years.” He said a second deposit, of P55 million, was handled the same way, bringing the total to P96 million.
Galvez’s records also showed four transfers of P20 million each from the Dutertes' joint account to BPI-Philam Life on March 28, 2014, for insurance plans worth P80 million in total.
A P16.85-million manager’s check from the same account was made out to "Samuel C. Uy" in May 2016, according to documents read out in court.

Sen. Tito Sotto, in his interjection, compared the alleged scheme to tinikling, the folk dance in which dancers dodge clapping bamboo poles. When Sen. Bam Aquino asked if it was a "known practice" among bankers, Galvez said it was “not uncommon” for clients to return unused checks.
Galvez said he could not tell the extent to which clients do it on purpose, but noted that purchasing managers' checks require them to state their reason for doing so in the application form.
Defense counsel Michael Poa claimed Duterte had no knowledge of the BPI joint account she had with her father and was only made aware of it during prior House hearings.

The joint account was also structured in a way that only the elder Duterte could transact alone, Poa pointed out, while Sara Duterte as co-depositor required her father's permission to move around any funds.
Poa also noted that the BPI records presented during the trial, including the P41.7-million manager's check, bore the signature of the former president and not Sara Duterte.
2. Millions in the bank, year after year
Bank witnesses put the couple’s combined year-end balances across eight banks at the following amounts, as summarized by the prosecution:

items: 2022: P59 million
2023: P71.3 million
2024: P22.2 million

blocks.text: On the flip side, the vice president declared zero cash on hand or in the bank for her SALNs from 2022 to 2024.
But the defense has long sought to debunk the allegation that Duterte misdeclared her wealth by explaining that cash on hand was grouped under "others" or "other personal properties" in her SALNs.

Based on the bank records cited by the prosecution, however, the Duterte couple's 2022 year-end balance of P59 million is more than four times the P13.325 million that was declared in “other personal properties” in the SALN that year.
Under cross-examination, the bank witnesses said they had no personal knowledge of the accounts and testified only from records produced under subpoena.

The Duterte couple kept at least 30 active accounts across eight banks from 2022 to 2025: LandBank, AUB, PSBank, Metrobank, Security Bank, BPI, PNB and BDO. These include accounts held jointly with other family members.
At BPI alone, Galvez counted seven active and 34 closed personal accounts, plus two credit card accounts and one corporate account.
3. Did Security Bank flag Cale88 transactions as suspicious?

Security Bank official Leslie Cham testified that Cale88 Foods Corporation, a declared business interest of Carpio, kept two peso checking accounts with the bank. One was opened in August 2024 and the other in October 2025. Both were closed in July 2026, the month the trial began.

Cham said Cale88’s account recorded P40.14 million in inflows and P40 million in outflows in 2024, and P6.27 million in inflows in 2025. The two accounts closed with balances of P332,530.95 and P21,164.27.
Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian then read from suspicious transaction reports on Cale88 as provided by the Anti-Money Laundering Council:

items: There were 12 cash deposits flagged as not matching Cale88 declared financial profile
Cale88 was flagged for failing to provide supporting documents and stopped responding to requests for clarification, so the bank could not verify where the money came from or what it was for.

blocks.text: Asked whether it was Security Bank that filed those reports, Cham said: “I cannot confirm.”
Cham invoked the confidentiality clause of the Anti-Money Laundering Act and said he could not say whether suspicious transaction records were indeed filed on Cale88.

Corporate records identify Cale88 as a Davao-based banana chips exporter. But the prosecution previously raised red flags about the firm, such as its low reported electricity bills, unusual for a food factory, as well as its large inward remittances from Chinese companies.
October 7 was the longest trial day yet, surpassing the previous record holder just two days before, which lasted around nine hours.
